Efficient learning of quantum states prepared with few fermionic non-Gaussian gates

Antonio Anna Mele Email: a.mele@fu-berlin.de Affiliation: Dahlem Center for Complex Quantum Systems, Freie Universität Berlin, 14195 Berlin, Germany    Yaroslav Herasymenko Email: yaroslav@cwi.nl Affiliation: QuSoft and CWI, Science Park 123, 1098 XG Amsterdam, The Netherlands Affiliation: QuTech, TU Delft, P.O. Box 5046, 2600 GA Delft, The Netherlands Affiliation: Delft Institute of Applied Mathematics, TU Delft, 2628 CD Delft, The Netherlands
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The experimental realization of increasingly complex quantum states underscores the pressing need for new methods of state learning and verification. In one such framework, quantum state tomography, the aim is to learn the full quantum state from data obtained by measurements. Without prior assumptions on the state, this task is prohibitively hard. Here, we present an efficient algorithm for learning states on nn fermion modes prepared by any number of Gaussian and at most tt non-Gaussian gates. By Jordan-Wigner mapping, this also includes nn-qubit states prepared by nearest-neighbour matchgate circuits with at most tt SWAP-gates. Our algorithm is based exclusively on single-copy measurements and produces a classical representation of a state, guaranteed to be close in trace distance to the target state. The sample and time complexity of our algorithm is poly⁡(n,2t)\mathrm{poly}(n,2^{t}); thus if t=𝒪⁡(log⁡(n))t=\mathcal{O}(\log(n)), it is efficient. We also show that, if tt scales slightly more than logarithmically, any learning algorithm to solve the same task must be inefficient, under common cryptographic assumptions. We also provide an efficient property testing algorithm that, given access to copies of a state, determines whether such a state is far or close to the set of states for which our learning algorithm works. In addition to the outputs of quantum circuits, our tomography algorithm is efficient for some physical target states, such as those arising in time dynamics and low-energy physics of impurity models. Beyond tomography, our work sheds light on the structure of states prepared with few non-Gaussian gates and offers an improved upper bound on their circuit complexity, enabling an efficient circuit compilation method.

I Introduction

Quantum state tomography is the task of reconstructing a classical description of a quantum state from experimental data [1, 2]. Beyond its foundational significance in quantum information theory, it stands as the gold standard for verification and benchmarking of quantum devices [2]. However, in the absence of any prior assumptions on the state to be learned, one encounters necessarily the curse of dimensionality of the Hilbert space: learning the classical description of a generic quantum state demands resources that grow exponentially with the number of qubits [1, 3]. Simply storing and outputting the density matrix of a state already results in an exponential cost in time. This raises the crucial question of identifying interesting classes of quantum states that can be efficiently learned using a number of state copies and time scaling at most polynomially with the system size. Only a few classes of states are currently known to be efficiently learnable — in particular, matrix product states [2, 4], finitely-correlated states [5], high-temperature Gibbs states [6], states prepared by shallow quantum circuits [7, 8, 9], stabilizer states [10], quantum phase states [11], and fermionic Gaussian states [12, 13]. The latter class of states comprises those prepared by fermionic Gaussian circuits [14], also referred to as free fermionic (non-interacting) evolutions or fermionic linear-optics circuits [15, 16]. Via Jordan-Wigner mapping, such states on nn fermionic modes can also be viewed as nn-qubit states, prepared by generalized matchgate circuits [16, 17, 18]. Fermionic Gaussian states states play a key role in condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry, via the Hartree-Fock method and in the context of Fermi Liquid and Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer theories [19, 20, 21, 22]. These states are also essential in understanding many exactly solvable spin models [23, 24, 25]. In quantum computing, fermionic Gaussian states are primarily recognized for their efficient classical simulability [15, 18, 17]. As in the case of Clifford circuits, for which the introduction of magic gates, such as T-gates, allows to reach universal quantum computation [26], also for the case of Gaussian circuits the inclusion of certain magic gates [27, 28, 29], for example SWAP gates [28], allows to reach universality. If the number tt of T-gates in a Clifford circuit is low, the resulting states can still be efficiently simulated classically [30, 31, 32]; it has also been recently demonstrated that such states, termed as tt-doped stabilizer states [33, 34], are still efficiently learnable [35, 36, 37]. Similarly, in the past year, it has been shown that Gaussian circuits with a few magic gates are also classically simulable [38, 39, 40]. However, the learnability of such “tt-doped fermionic Gaussian states” remains unknown and this motivates the core-question of our work:

Can we efficiently learn states prepared by Gaussian operations (e.g. matchgates) and a few magic gates?

We answer it by proposing a quantum algorithm of polynomial time and sample complexity that uses only single-copy measurements and learns a succint classical description of a tt-doped fermionic Gaussian state; the learned state is guaranteed to be close to the true state in trace distance. Our presentation is framed in the language of qubits, but the results seamlessly translate into the fermionic formalism. Our learning algorithm may also be feasible to implement in near-term fermionic analog quantum simulators [41, 42], like cold atoms in optical lattices [43], since we only utilize time evolutions of simple few-body fermionic Hamiltonians [44]. The core of our algorithm relies on a result of independent interest, elucidating the structure of states in question. In particular, for any tt-doped fermionic Gaussian state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} we show that there exists a Gaussian operation GG such that G†​|ψ⟩=|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−κ​t⟩,G^{\dagger}\ket{\psi}=\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-\kappa t}}, where |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is supported on κ​t\kappa t qubits and κ\kappa is a small constant. Informally, this says that all the magic (non-Gaussianity) of such states can be compressed to a few qubits via a Gaussian operation. The proof of our compression theorem is constructive, which has implications for the circuit complexity of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} and for improved preparation of doped fermionic Gaussian states.

The high level idea of the learning algorithm is to first learn a Gaussian unitary GG which compresses the magic, apply it to the state, and then perform full state state tomography on the first few qubits alone. Our learning algorithm has a time complexity 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n,2t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(n,2^{t})), i.e. it scales polynomially in the system size nn and exponentially in the number of non-Gaussian gates tt. Thus it is efficient as long as the number of non-Gaussian gates is t=𝒪⁡(log⁡(n))t=\mathcal{O}(\log(n)). Furthermore, we establish that the task of learning such states is computationally intractable when the number of non-Gaussian gates scales slightly more than logarithmically, under a common cryptography assumption [46, 47, 48, 49]. We show the latter result using the theory of pseudorandom quantum states [50, 51] and qubit-to-fermion mappings [25]. In doing that, we bring pseudorandom quantum states, so far explored only for qubit-based systems, to the fermionic realm. Our learning algorithm generalizes the one presented by Aaronson et al. [12], which is tailored to learn only those states prepared by particle-number conserving Gaussian gates and t=0t=0 (in our work we relax both of these assumptions).

Furthermore, our algorithm extends to all Gaussian compressible states, i.e., those states which can be written as G⁡(σ⊗|0n−t⟩⟨0n−t|)​G†G(\sigma\otimes\outerproduct{0^{n-t}}{0^{n-t}})G^{{\dagger}}, where GG is a Gaussian unitary and σ\sigma is a possibly mixed quantum state supported on the first tt qubits. We also propose an efficient method to test if a given state is close or far from the set of compressible states, by showing an efficiently estimatable quantity that lower bounds the distance to this set. Moreover, we also demonstrate that our learning algorithm can learn states that are close to being compressible – this feature is particularly significant as it emphasizes the noise-robustness of the algorithm. Additionally, we note that ground states of impurity models, a well-regarded class of quantum states in condensed matter physics [52, 53, 54, 45], are approximately compressible, making our algorithm suitable for efficient tomography of such physically relevant states. We further provide numerical evidence showing that states prepared by time evolutions governed by impurity model Hamiltonians [45] remain approximately compressible until constant evolution times, thus making them learnable by our tomography algorithm.

It should be noted that the concept of magic compression was first introduced in the context of Clifford+T circuits by Leone, Oliviero et al. [55, 56] and later exploited for learning tt-doped stabilizer states [35, 36]. Our strategy of proving non-Gaussianity compression and applying it to quantum state tomography was inspired by these earlier works. It is an intriguing fact that a similar compression theorem holds in our context, even though the mathematical structures of stabilizer states and fermionic Gaussian states appear quite different.

See Figure 1 for the visual summary of our results. In the next sections we summarize our findings, stating more precisely our results and the essential ideas that underlie them. In the Supplementary Material, we provide the technical details.

I.1 Preliminaries

Our work can be applied to two distinct and naively separate settings: a system of nn qubits with 1D matchgates circuits and their magic gates (e.g., SWAP gates), or a native fermionic system of nn modes with states prepared by fermionic Gaussian evolutions and local non-Gaussian evolutions. These two perspectives are mathematically related through the Jordan-Wigner mapping. We will use it now as a definition of Majorana operators, thus directly aligning our discussion with the qubit language. Majorana operators, denoted as γ2​k−1\gamma_{2k-1} and γ2​k\gamma_{2k} for k∈[n]≔{1,…,n}k\in[n]\coloneqq\{1,\dots,n\}, are defined in terms of standard Pauli operators as γ2​k−1≔(∏j=1k−1Zj)​Xk\gamma_{2k-1}\coloneqq(\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}Z_{j})X_{k} and γ2​k≔(∏j=1k−1Zj)​Yk\gamma_{2k}\coloneqq(\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}Z_{j})Y_{k}. Alternatively, they can be defined in the fermionic language through their anticommutation relations [15, 57]. A fermionic Gaussian unitary GG is a unitary that satisfies G†​γμ​G=∑ν=12​nOμ,ν​γνG^{\dagger}\gamma_{\mu}G=\sum^{2n}_{\nu=1}O_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_{\nu} for any μ∈[2​n]\mu\in[2n], where O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n) is an orthogonal matrix. The product of two Gaussian unitaries is Gaussian. Notably, a one-to-one correspondence exists between Gaussian unitaries up to a global phase and O⁡(2​n)\mathrm{O}(2n) orthogonal matrices. Given an orthogonal matrix, it is known how to exactly implement the associated Gaussian unitary using 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) 22-local qubits or 22-local fermionic Gaussian operations [58, 38, 59]. A pure fermionic Gaussian state can be defined as |ψ⟩=G​|0n⟩\ket{\psi}=G\ket{0^n}, where GG is a Gaussian unitary and |0n⟩\ket{0^n} denotes the zero computational basis state. Given a quantum state ρ\rho, its correlation matrix C⁡(ρ)C(\rho) is defined as the real anti-symmetric 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n matrix with elements [C⁡(ρ)]j,k≔−i2​Tr⁡(γj​γk​ρ)[C(\rho)]_{j,k}\coloneqq-\frac{i}{2}\Tr\left(\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k}\rho\right), for any j<k∈[2​n]j<k\in[2n]. We have that C⁡(G​ρ​G†)=O​C​(ρ)​OTC(G\rho G^{\dagger})=OC(\rho)O^{T}, for any Gaussian unitary GG associated with O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n). A well-known result in linear algebra [60] asserts that any real anti-symmetric matrix CC can be decomposed in the so-called ‘normal form’:

C=O​⨁j=1n(0λj−λj0)​OT,\displaystyle C=O\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}0&\lambda_{j}\\ -\lambda_{j}&0\end{pmatrix}O^{T}, (1)

where OO is an orthogonal matrix in O⁡(2​n)\mathrm{O}(2n) and λj≥0\lambda_{j}\geq 0, for any j∈[n]j\in[n], are dubbed as ‘normal’ eigenvalues, ordered in increasing order. We denote the trace distance between two quantum states |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} and |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} as dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕ⟩)≔12​‖|ψ⟩⟨ψ|−|ϕ⟩⟨ϕ|‖1d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi})\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\norm{\ketbra{\psi}-\ketbra{\phi}}_{1}. Given a matrix AA, its operator norm ‖A‖∞\norm{A}_{\infty} is defined as its largest singular value. We refer to the Supplementary Material (SM) for more preliminaries.

I.2 Structure of tt-doped Gaussian states

States prepared by Gaussian circuits applied to a computational basis state are efficiently simulable classically. However, by incorporating ‘non-Gaussian’, or ‘magic’ operations, such as SWAP\operatorname{SWAP}-gates [28, 17], one can render Gaussian circuits universal for quantum computation. The term ‘magic gate’ comes from a loose parallel to Clifford circuits, which are efficiently simulable per se but become universal upon introduction of ‘magic’ non-Clifford T\operatorname{T}-gates.

Here we consider non-Gaussian operations generated by κ\kappa Majorana operators {γμ⁡(r)}r=1κ\{\gamma_{\mu(r)}\}^{\kappa}_{r=1}, where μ⁡(1),…,μ⁡(κ)∈[2​n]\mu(1),\dots,\mu(\kappa)\in[2n]. Examples of such non-Gaussian operations for κ=4\kappa=4 are the SWAP\operatorname{SWAP}-gate or a unitary exp⁡(i​θ​γ1​γ5​γ6​γ8)\exp\!\left(i\theta\gamma_{1}\gamma_{5}\gamma_{6}\gamma_{8}\right) for θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R}; for κ=3\kappa=3, an example is exp⁡(θ​γ2​γ6​γ7)\exp\!\left(\theta\gamma_{2}\gamma_{6}\gamma_{7}\right). We refer to κ\kappa as the maximum Majorana locality of the employed non-Gaussian gates.

Definition 1 (tt-doped fermionic Gaussian state).

A state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is a (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped Gaussian state if it can be prepared by Gaussian unitaries {Gi}i=0t\{G_{i}\}^{t}_{i=0} and tt non-Gaussian κ\kappa-local gates {Wi}i=1t\{W_{i}\}^{t}_{i=1}, specifically

|ψ⟩=GtWt⋯G1W1G0|0n⟩,\displaystyle\ket{\psi}=G_{t}W_{t}\cdots G_{1}W_{1}G_{0}\ket{0^n}, (2)

where κ\kappa-local means that each non-Gaussian gate involves at most κ\kappa Majorana operators. Informally, a state is tt-doped Gaussian if it is (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped Gaussian for some fixed constant κ\kappa.

Similarly, we denote the unitary Ut≔GtWt⋯G1W1G0U_{t}\coloneqq G_{t}W_{t}\cdots G_{1}W_{1}G_{0} as a tt-doped Gaussian unitary. We now present our main result concerning the structure of tt-doped Gaussian states: it is possible to compress all the ‘non-Gaussianity’ of the state into a localized region of the system via a Gaussian operation. This motivates the following definition.

Definition 2 (tt-compressible Gaussian state).

Let t∈[n]t\in[n]. A state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is (Gaussian) tt-compressible if and only if

|ψ⟩=G⁡(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩),\displaystyle\ket{\psi}=G(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n- t}}), (3)

where GG is a Gaussian operation, and |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is a state supported solely on the first tt qubits.

In the following, we assume κ​t≤n\kappa t\leq n.

Theorem 3 (Magic compression in tt-doped Gaussian states).

Any (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped Gaussian state is κ​t\kappa t-compressible.

Proof sketch.

Let Ut​|0n⟩U_{t}\ket{0^n} be the tt-doped state, where Ut=(∏t′=1tGt′​Wt′)​G0U_{t}=(\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}G_{t^{\prime}}W_{t^{\prime}})G_{0} is the tt-doped unitary. We rearrange UtU_{t} as Ut=G~t​Gaux​∏t′=1t(Gaux†​W~t′​Gaux)​Gaux†U_{t}=\tilde{G}_{t}G_{\mathrm{aux}}\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}(G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}G_{\mathrm{aux}})G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}, introducing a Gaussian operation GauxG_{\mathrm{aux}} to be fixed and defining W~t′≔G~t′−1†​Wt′​G~t′−1\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}\coloneqq\tilde{G}^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}-1}W_{t^{\prime}}\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}-1} and G~t′≔Gt′..G0\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}}\coloneqq G_{t^{\prime}}..G_{0}. We require that GauxG_{\mathrm{aux}} satisfies Gaux†​|0n⟩=|0n⟩G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\ket{0^n}=\ket{0^n}, and that each Gaux†​W~t′​GauxG^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}G_{\mathrm{aux}} is supported non-trivially only on the first κ​t\kappa t qubits. The latter is enforced by demanding that the Heisenberg evolution, via G~t′−1​Gaux\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}-1}G_{\mathrm{aux}}, of each Majorana operator involved in the Hamiltonian generating Wt′W_{t^{\prime}}, has non-trivial support exclusively on the first κ​t\kappa t qubits. The existence of GauxG_{\mathrm{aux}} is shown by demonstrating the existence of its associated orthogonal matrix OauxO_{\mathrm{aux}}. The requirements on GauxG_{\mathrm{aux}} translate into the demand that OauxO_{\mathrm{aux}} must be symplectic and such that it sends κ​t\kappa t fixed vectors to the span of the first 2​κ​t2\kappa t canonical basis vectors. The existence of such OauxO_{\mathrm{aux}} can be proven via the isomorphism between real 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n symplectic orthogonal matrices and n×nn\times n unitaries [61]. Additional details are provided in the Supplementary Material (see Theorem 27). ∎

This compressibility should not be confused with the compressed quantum computation result described in Ref. [62], which pertains to free-fermionic circuits (t=0t=0) and demonstrates how such computations can be equivalently expressed in logarithmic space.

Note that while a (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped Gaussian state is a κ​t\kappa t-compressible Gaussian state, the reverse implication does not hold due to circuit complexity arguments. Similarly to Theorem 3, we show that any tt-doped Gaussian unitary can be represented as:

Ut=GA​(ut⊗I)​GB,\displaystyle U_{t}=G_{A}(u_{t}\otimes I)G_{B}, (4)

where GAG_{A} and GBG_{B} denote Gaussian operations, and utu_{t} is a unitary operator supported on ⌈κ​t/2⌉\lceil\kappa t/2\rceil qubits (with ⌈⋅⌉\lceil\cdot\rceil denoting rounding to the next integer), as elaborated in the Supplementary Material (Theorem 26). Notably, if UtU_{t} is a particle number conserving unitary [15], then GAG_{A}, utu_{t} and GBG_{B} can also be chosen as such.

Our proof of Theorem 3 is constructive, i.e., given a classical description of the circuit that prepares |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}, it provides an efficient procedure for finding the compressing Gaussian circuit GG and the state |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi}. The decomposition of tt-doped Gaussian states (unitaries) reveals also that they have a circuit complexity, i.e., number of local gates needed for implementing the state (unitary), upper bounded by 𝒪⁡(n2+t3)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+t^{3}) (Proposition 30 in SM). This provides a better circuit complexity upper bound compared to the naive 𝒪⁡(n2​t)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}t) implied by definition 1 for κ=𝒪⁡(1)\kappa=\mathcal{O}(1). Hence, our construction reveals also a method to compress the circuit depth (and not only the magic), which might be used in practice for efficient circuit compilation of doped matchgate circuits. Remarkably, analogous results hold for the Clifford+T gates circuits [56].

In the context of Clifford operations, the notions of stabilizer dimension [35] and stabilizer nullity [63, 64] were introduced to quantify the degree of stabilizerness of a quantum state, and their connection to magic monotones was investigated. Analogously, we define the Gaussian dimension of a state as the number of normal eigenvalues of its correlation matrix that are equal to one, and the Gaussian nullity as the number of normal eigenvalues of its correlation matrix that are strictly less than one.

Using Eq. (1), we can show that a state has a Gaussian nullity of at most tt (a Gaussian dimension of at least n−tn-t) if and only if it is tt-compressible. Consequently, (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped Gaussian states have a Gaussian nullity of at most κ​t\kappa t (a Gaussian dimension of at least n−κ​tn-\kappa t).

I.3 Learning Algorithm

We present an algorithm for learning tt-compressible Gaussian states, or, equivalently, quantum states with at least n−tn-t Gaussian dimension. Note that this is a broader class than tt-doped Gaussian states; as an example unrelated to tt-doped states, ground states of quantum impurity models are approximately of this form (as shown in [45] and elaborated further in the subsequent subsections). By definition, any tt-compressible Gaussian state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} can be factorized as G†​|ψ⟩=|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩G^{{\dagger}}\ket{\psi}=\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}, where G†G^{{\dagger}} is Gaussian and |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is a state on tt qubits. At a high level, our strategy is to learn the Gaussian unitary G†G^{{\dagger}}, apply it to |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}, and then perform full state tomography solely on the first tt qubits to learn |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi}. Since full state tomography algorithms scale exponentially with the number of qubits [65], for t=𝒪⁡(log⁡(n))t=\mathcal{O}(\log(n)) our algorithm will be efficient.

To delve deeper, the initial phase of our learning algorithm entails estimating the correlation matrix entries through single-copy measurements. This can be achieved using different methods outlined in the Supplementary Material, such as measurements in the Pauli basis, global Clifford Gaussian measurements [66], or fermionic classical shadows [58, 67, 68]. The estimated correlation matrix C^\hat{C} is subsequently transformed into its normal form in Eq.(1) to yield the corresponding orthogonal matrix O^\hat{O} associated with the Gaussian operation G^\hat{G}. (We use the hat symbol to denote the objects estimated from the measurements.) Applying the inverse operation G^†\hat{G}^{{\dagger}} to |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} results in a state that exhibits high fidelity with a state, which is tensor product of an arbitrary state on the first tt qubits and the zero computational basis state on the remaining n−tn-t qubits. Consequently, the learning algorithm queries multiple copies of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} (one at a time), applies G^†\hat{G}^{{\dagger}} to them and measures the last n−tn-t qubits. If the outcome of such measurements correspond to |0n−t⟩\ket{0^{n-t}}, then the algorithm proceeds with a step of pure state tomography [65, 69] on the tt-qubits state. The state tomography routine performed in the compressed space yields the state |ϕ^⟩|\hat{\phi}\rangle. The final output of the learning algorithm is |ψ^⟩≔G^​(|ϕ^⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)|\hat{\psi}\rangle\coloneqq\hat{G}(|\hat{\phi}\rangle\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}), and an efficient classical representation can be provided if t=𝒪⁡(log⁡(n))t=\mathcal{O}(\log(n)). Namely, to specify |ψ^⟩|\hat{\psi}\rangle, it is sufficient to provide the complete description of the tt-qubit state |ϕ^⟩|\hat{\phi}\rangle and the orthogonal matrix O^∈O⁡(2​n)\hat{O}\in\mathrm{O}(2n) associated with G^\hat{G}.

We now present a theorem which formalizes and proves the efficiency of the discussed procedure, outlined in Algorithm 1, to learn doped Gaussian states or, more generally, tt-compressible Gaussian states.

Theorem 4 (Learning algorithm guarantees).

Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be a tt-compressible Gaussian state, and ε,δ∈(0,1]\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1]. Utilizing 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n,2t))\mathcal{O}\!\left(\mathrm{poly}\!\left(n,2^{t}\right)\right) single-copy measurements and computational time, Algorithm 1 outputs a classical representation of a state |ψ^⟩|\hat{\psi}\rangle, such that dtr​(|ψ^⟩,|ψ⟩)≤εd_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\psi}\rangle,\ket{\psi})\leq\varepsilon with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta.

Proof sketch.

Using 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(n)) copies of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}, we estimate its correlation matrix CC, yielding C^\hat{C} such that ‖C^−C‖∞≤εc\|\hat{C}-C\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon_{c} with a failure probability ≤δ3\leq\frac{\delta}{3}, where εc≔ε2/(4​(n−t))\varepsilon_{c}\coloneqq\varepsilon^{2}/(4(n-t)). Expressing C^\hat{C} in its normal form (Eq.(1)), we find the Gaussian unitary G^\hat{G} associated to O^∈O⁡(2​n)\hat{O}\in\mathrm{O}(2n). Let |ψ′⟩≔G^†​|ψ⟩\ket{\psi^{\prime}}\coloneqq\hat{G}^{{\dagger}}\ket{\psi}. As detailed in the Supplementary Material, we derive ⟨ψ′|​Zk​|ψ′⟩≥1−2​εc\bra{\psi^{\prime}}Z_{k}\ket{\psi^{\prime}}\geq 1-2\varepsilon_{c} for each k∈{t+1,…,n}k\in\{t+1,\dots,n\} and, by Quantum Union Bound [70] we get dtr​(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩,|ψ′⟩)≤ε2d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}},\ket{\psi^{\prime}})\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}, where |ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}} corresponds to the state obtained by measuring the last n−tn-t qubits of G^†​|ψ⟩\hat{G}^{{\dagger}}\ket{\psi} in the computational basis and obtaining the outcome corresponding to |0n−t⟩\ket{0^{n-t}}, an event which occurs with probability ≥1−ε2/4\geq 1-\varepsilon^{2}/4. By querying ⌈2​Ntom​(t,ε2,δ3)+24​log⁡(3δ)⌉\lceil 2N_{\mathrm{tom}}(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{3})+24\log(\frac{3}{\delta})\rceil copies of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}, and, for each copy, applying G^†\hat{G}^{{\dagger}} and measuring the last n−tn-t qubits, we get the outcome |0n−t⟩\ket{0^{n-t}} at least Ntom​(t,ε2,δ3)N_{\mathrm{tom}}(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{3}) times, with failure probability ≤δ3\leq\frac{\delta}{3} due to Chernoff bound. Here, Ntom​(t,ε2,δ3)N_{\mathrm{tom}}(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{3}) is the number of copies sufficient for full state tomography [65] of a tt-qubit state with an ε2\frac{\varepsilon}{2} accuracy and a failure probability ≤δ3\leq\frac{\delta}{3}. Performing the tt-qubit tomography on all the copies where the outcome |0n−t⟩\ket{0^{n-t}} occurred yields |ϕ^⟩|\hat{\phi}\rangle such that dtr​(|ϕ^⟩,|ϕ⟩)≤ε2d_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\phi}\rangle,\ket{\phi})\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}, with a failure probability ≤δ3\leq\frac{\delta}{3}. Defining |ψ^⟩≔G^​(|ϕ^⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)|\hat{\psi}\rangle\coloneqq\hat{G}(|\hat{\phi}\rangle\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}), we have dtr​(|ψ^⟩,|ψ⟩)≤dtr​(|ϕ^⟩,|ϕ⟩)+dtr​(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩,G^†​|ψ⟩)d_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\psi}\rangle,\ket{\psi})\leq d_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\phi}\rangle,\ket{\phi})+d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}},\hat{G}^{{\dagger}}\ket{\psi}). This is ≤ε\leq\varepsilon if the algorithm does not fail, an event occurring with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta due to the union bound. ∎

Theorem 4 is re-stated and rigorously proven in the Supplemental Material as Theorem 44. The sample, time and memory complexity of our algorithm for learning tt-compressible states exhibits a polynomial dependence on nn and an exponential dependence on tt: specifically, the poly⁡(n)\mathrm{poly}(n) contribution (specifically an 𝒪⁡(n5)\mathcal{O}(n^{5}) scaling) arises solely from estimating and post-processing the correlation matrix, while the exp⁡(t)\mathrm{exp}(t) contribution arises from full state tomography on tt-qubits. It is easy to see that the dependence on tt is optimal, because learning tt-compressible states is at least as hard as learning an arbitrary pure state on tt qubits and thus requires at least exp⁡(Ω⁡(t))\exp(\Omega(t)) copies of the state [3].

However, if we focus on the subclass of tt-doped Gaussian states, a classical shadow tomography based algorithm presented in [71, 72] achieves 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n,t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(n,t)) sample complexity. Specifically, this algorithm requires a number of copies that scales polynomially with the circuit complexity of the state, and tt-doped states have a circuit complexity 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n,t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(n,t)). However, the time complexity of the algorithm in [71, 72] scales exponentially with the number of qubits nn, while our algorithm’s time complexity scales only polynomially (although always exponentially in tt). This observation also applies to tt-doped stabilizer states learning analyzed in recent works [36, 35].

In our Supplementary Material, we extend our learning algorithm to handle mixed states. Specifically, we provide an algorithm to learn, in trace distance, possibly mixed quantum states that have at least n−tn-t normal eigenvalues of their correlation matrix equal to one. In the more general mixed state scenario, the algorithm in Table 1 becomes significantly simpler. Notably, measuring the last n−tn-t qubits and post-selecting on the outcome |0n−t⟩\ket{0^{n-t}} is not necessary, as we do not require the output state to be pure. Thus, it is sufficient to perform full state tomography [1] on the first tt qubits right after the Gaussian operation G^†\hat{G}^{\dagger} is applied to the state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}. More details are given in Section VII of the appendix.

Additionally, in Section VII, we analyze the noise robustness of our algorithm, which is crucial for practical experimental scenarios where the unknown state may not be exactly tt-compressible, but approximately so. Specifically, our analysis reveals that our algorithm allows for efficient tomography of states that are possibly mixed and (sufficiently) approximately compressible, which are the types of states one would expect to get when running a tt-doped matchgate circuit on a noisy quantum device.

I.4 Time complexity lower bound

It is natural to wonder whether there exist algorithms for learning tt-doped Gaussian states with time complexity scaling in tt as 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(t)). We establish that the answer is no (see Proposition 50 in SM), relying on a widely-believed cryptography assumption. Specifically, we show that certain families of pseudorandom quantum states [51, 50] can be generated using a polynomial number of local non-Gaussian gates. This implies that if there were an algorithm with polynomial time complexity in tt for learning tt-doped Gaussian states, quantum computers could solve 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} [73] in polynomial time, which is considered unlikely [73, 74, 46, 47, 75, 48]. While this rules out the existence of efficient algorithms if tt scales polynomially with the number of qubits nn, it does not yet preclude the existence of efficient algorithms if tt grows slightly more than logarithmically, for example t=𝒪⁡((log⁡n)2)t=\mathcal{O}((\log n)^{2}). However, we can rule out this possibility by making the stronger assumption that quantum computers cannot solve 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} in sub-exponential time [46, 47, 48, 49]. This implies that the time complexity of any algorithm to learn 𝒪~​(t)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(t)-doped Gaussian states (where 𝒪~​(⋅)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot) hides polylogarithmic factors) would necessarily be exp⁡(Ω⁡(t))\exp(\Omega(t)). In other words, the following holds.

Theorem 5 (Time-complexity lower bound, informal).

Assuming that quantum computers cannot solve 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} in sub-exponential time, then there is no time efficient algorithm to learn ω~​(log⁡(n))\tilde{\omega}(\log(n))-doped Gaussian state which outputs a description of an efficiently preparable quantum state. Here, ω~​(log⁡(n))≔ω⁡(log⁡(n)​polyloglog​(n))\tilde{\omega}(\log(n))\coloneqq\omega\!\left(\log(n)\mathrm{polyloglog}(n)\right).

This would prove that the time complexity in tt of our algorithm is essentially optimal, because our algorithm is efficient as long as t=𝒪⁡(log⁡(n))t=\mathcal{O}(\log(n)). We show Theorem 5 by efficiently encoding the pseudorandom quantum states constructions [72] via a specific qubits-to-fermions mapping [25] into other states produced by the same number of gates, all of which are now local non-Gaussian. Crucially for our construction, this mapping sends local qubit operations to local fermionic operations with only a constant overhead in the number of qubits. We refer the reader to the Supplementary Material (Proposition 52) for more details.

I.5 Testing Gaussian dimension

We have introduced an algorithm for efficiently learning states with a high Gaussian dimension (or, equivalently, small Gaussian nullity), specifically those promised to be tt-compressible with a small tt. A natural question arises: How can we test the Gaussian dimension of a state? In other words, how can we determine if the underlying state is close or far from the set of tt-compressible states? In our Supplementary Material, using ideas developed in [76] for the case of Gaussian states (t=0t=0), we establish that the minimum trace distance between a quantum state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} and the set of tt-compressible Gaussian states, denoted by 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}, satisfies:

1−λt+12≤min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≤∑k=t+1n1−λk2,\displaystyle\frac{1-\lambda_{t+1}}{2}\leq\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\leq\sqrt{\sum^{n}_{k=t+1}\frac{1-\lambda_{k}}{2}}, (5)

where {λk}k=1n\{\lambda_{k}\}^{n}_{k=1} represents the normal eigenvalues of the correlation matrix of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} ordered in increasing order. These inequalities imply that |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is close in trace distance to the set 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} if and only if λt+1\lambda_{t+1} is close to one. In particular, assuming that |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is either a state in 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} or min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≥ε\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\geq\varepsilon, we can determine with at least 1−δ1-\delta probability which of the two cases is true by accurately estimating λt+1\lambda_{t+1}. Specifically, 𝒪⁡((n5/ε4)​log⁡(n2/δ))\mathcal{O}((n^{5}/\varepsilon^{4})\log(n^2/\delta)) copies of the state suffice for this purpose. Notably, this complexity scaling for testing is independent from tt, in contrast to learning. More details are provided in section V of the Supplementary Material, along with a generalization to the mixed-state scenario.

I.6 Numerical simulations: tt-compressible states in many-body physics

In the previous section, we introduced an algorithm to learn quantum states that are tt-compressible. In Section VII of the Supplementary Material, we extended the algorithm to learn states that are not exactly tt-compressible but approximately. This connects to the work of Bravyi and Gosset [45], who demonstrated that ground states of so-called quantum impurity models can be well-approximated by compressible states (see Ref. [45], Corollary 1). In this section we discuss the learnability of such states and of the states produced by the time dynamics of impurity models.

Quantum impurity models represent a bath of free fermions coupled with a small localized interacting subsystem referred to as an impurity. These models are of paramount importance in condensed matter physics and have been extensively studied over the past half-century. The exploration of such Hamiltonians gained significant traction in the 1960s and 70s, largely due to the pioneering work of Anderson, Kondo, and Wilson. Their focus was on the behavior of magnetic impurities within metals [54, 52, 77, 53], providing a theoretical basis for the Kondo effect [53], which had been experimentally observed much earlier. Quantum impurity models are also crucial computational tools for analyzing the electronic structure of strongly correlated materials, including transition metal compounds and high-temperature superconductors. They are integral to the dynamical mean field theory (DMFT) [78], a method used to study these materials. In DMFT, the impurity typically represents a cluster of atoms within a unit cell, while the bath models the bulk of the material.

Formally, a quantum impurity model Hamiltonian is a Hamiltonian HmH_{m} that can be expressed as Hm=Hfree+Himp,mH_{m}=H_{\mathrm{free}}+H_{\mathrm{imp},m}, where HfreeH_{\mathrm{free}} is a free-fermionic Hamiltonian (i.e., a Hamiltonian quadratic in the Majorana operators Hfree=i​∑p,q=12​nhp,q​γp​γqH_{\mathrm{free}}=i\sum_{p,q=1}^{2n}h_{p,q}\gamma_{p}\gamma_{q}, with hh being a real anti-symmetric matrix) and Himp,mH_{\mathrm{imp},m} is an arbitrary Hamiltonian, potentially non-free fermionic, acting non-trivially on at most mm distinct Majorana operators, where mm is chosen to be O⁡(1)O(1) relative to the number of fermionic modes nn.

Restating Corollary 1 from Ref. [45], Bravyi and Gosset demonstrated that ground states |ψGS⟩\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{GS}}} of impurity models can be approximated, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, by a tt-compressible Gaussian state with t≔O⁡(log⁡(ε−1))t\coloneqq O(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})). Specifically, there exists a Gaussian unitary GG and a state |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} supported on tt modes such that ‖ψGS−ψt‖1≤ε\norm{\psi_{\mathrm{GS}} - \psi_t}_{1}\leq\varepsilon, where |ψt⟩≔G⁡(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)\ket{\psi_t}\coloneqq G(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}) 11 1 The asymptotic notation t=O⁡(log⁡(ε−1))t=O(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})) hides a logarithmic dependence on the inverse of the spectral gap of the free-fermionic Hamiltonian HfreeH_{\mathrm{free}}. For more details, see Ref. [45].. Thus, our algorithm can effectively be applied to learn ground states of impurity models with arbitrary ε\varepsilon-precision, with a sample complexity scaling as poly⁡(n,ε−1)\mathrm{poly}(n,\varepsilon^{-1}).

An intriguing question arises: can evolutions governed by such Hamiltonians maintain approximate tt-compressibility up to certain evolution times, thus making our algorithm applicable to such non-equilibrium quantum states? To explore this, we conducted numerical simulations with an interacting impurity embedded in the background of two distinct free models: the 1D transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) and an expander graph model. The respective Hamiltonians are HTFIM=w​Z1​Z2+∑j=1n(g​Xj​Xmod​(j+1,n)+Zj)H_{\mathrm{TFIM}}=wZ_{1}Z_{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}(gX_{j}X_{\text{mod}(j+1,n)}+Z_{j}), where ww and gg are real numbers, and Hgraph=w​γ1​γ2​γ3​γ4+∑e∈𝒢i​ve​γe⁡(1)​γe⁡(2)H_{\mathrm{graph}}=w\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}\gamma_{4}+\sum_{e\in\mathcal{G}}iv_{e}\gamma_{e(1)}\gamma_{e(2)}, where 𝒢\mathcal{G} represents a random 4-regular graph, with coupling constants vev_{e} uniformly set to 1 for simplicity. Without the impurity term (i.e., for w=0w=0), both Hamiltonians become quadratic in the Majorana operators (up to a long ZZ-string term, corresponding to a fixed parity contribution), implying that the continuous evolution they realize is Gaussian. We focus on the cases g=w=1g=w=1, so that the energy scales of the impurity term and the quadratic part are comparable.

We consider the continuous evolution |ψ⁡(T)⟩=e−i​H​T​|0n⟩\ket{\psi(T)}=e^{-iHT}\ket{0^n} with H=HgraphH=H_{\mathrm{graph}} and HTFIMH_{\mathrm{TFIM}} and investigate whether the resulting state |ψ⁡(T)⟩\ket{\psi(T)} is approximately tt-compressible. To determine this, we check if there exists a tt such that

∑m=t+1n12​(1−λm)≤εtrunc,\sqrt{\sum_{m=t+1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}(1-\lambda_{m})}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{trunc}}, (6)

where {λj}j=1n\{\lambda_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n} are the normal eigenvalues of the correlation matrix of |ψ⁡(T)⟩\ket{\psi(T)} ordered in increasing order, and εtrunc\varepsilon_{\mathrm{trunc}} is a fixed truncation error, which captures the approximate tt-compressiblity of the underlying quantum state. This implies that the state |ψ⁡(T)⟩\ket{\psi(T)} can be learned with our algorithm up to an error ε+εtrunc\varepsilon+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{trunc}} in trace distance, where ε\varepsilon is the accuracy chosen in the tomography algorithm (see Theorem 57 of the Supplementary material for more details). This learning error can be brought closer to εtrunc\varepsilon_{\mathrm{trunc}} by decreasing ε\varepsilon at the respective cost. In Figure 2, we present the dynamics of the minimal Gaussian nullity tt that allows a compression error below εtrunc=0.05\varepsilon_{\mathrm{trunc}}=0.05, as a function of the evolution time TT.

For small evolution times TT, as shown in Figure 2 (left panel), |ψ⁡(T)⟩\ket{\psi(T)} exhibits small approximate Gaussian nullity. One might wonder if this approximate tt-compressibility of impurity dynamics scales well with the system size, or whether, on the contrary, maintaining a fixed error in trace distance becomes increasingly difficult for larger nn. Our numerical analysis suggests the former. For instance, consider the maximal time T4T_{4} that allows maintaining approximate tt-compressibility for t=4t=4 and a fixed εtrunc\varepsilon_{\mathrm{trunc}}. The question is whether T4T_{4} decreases to zero with increasing nn or stabilizes at a constant value. We find that T4T_{4} indeed saturates at a certain constant for both the TFIM and the expander models (Figure 2, right panel).

We also examine whether the compressibility shown in Figure 2 can be derived from our Theorem 3 for tt-doped circuits using the Trotter approximation. Our numerical analysis rules out this gate-counting hypothesis, because this hypothesis predicts high approximate nullity already for minuscule times (vertical dotted lines in Figure 2, left panel). A detailed explanation of this analysis is given in Section VIII of the Supplementary Material. We do not have an analytical derivation of approximate tt-compressibility of impurity dynamics as observed in our numerical investigation, and leave this question open for future work. The failure of explanation via Trotter expansion highlights the difficulty of this problem. For the TFIM model, the approximate tt-compressibility may be derivable using 1D Lieb-Robinson bounds. However, such a derivation should not work for the expander graph model – and at present we do not know how this case could be analytically handled. This open problem also connects to the open questions about the classical simulation of impurity dynamics, raised earlier by Bravyi and Gosset [45].

To run the simulations of |ψ⁡(T)⟩=e−i​H​T​|0n⟩\ket{\psi(T)}=e^{-iHT}\ket{0^n} presented in Figure 2, we employed sparse matrix multiplication routines. More details about our numerical simulations are given in Section VIII of the Supplementary Material.

I.7 Conclusions

In this work, we have presented an algorithm for efficiently learning tt-doped fermionic Gaussian states, with sample and time complexity scaling as 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n,2t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(n,2^{t})). Additionally, we have established, under standard cryptography assumptions, that there is no learning algorithm for such class of states with a polynomial dependence on tt in the time complexity. Crucially, our algorithm utilizes solely experimentally feasible single-copy measurements. Its working idea is based on a theorem that we prove, which says that all the non-Gaussianity in a tt-doped fermionic Gaussian state can be efficiently compressed onto 𝒪⁡(t)\mathcal{O}(t) qubits through a Gaussian operation. This observation carries potential significance beyond the scope of learning, particularly within the context of quantum many-body theory or within efficient circuit compilation. Thus, the results presented in this work, besides being directly relevant to device verification and benchmarking, among other tasks, hold fundamental significance for quantum information theory, as they reveal more about the structure of Gaussian states with fermionic magic gates. Additionally, we introduce a variety of useful analytical techniques, such as new ways to leverage pseudo-random quantum states [51, 50] in the context of fermionic systems, which are likely to find applications in future research. We also observe that the results presented in our study for fermionic systems have already found application in continuous variable systems and bosonic Gaussian states [80], where the concept of tt-doped bosonic Gaussian states is explored, highlighting the broader applicability of our ideas and techniques to a different context.

Our work offers new directions for further research. An open question arising from this work is whether tt-doped Gaussian unitaries can be efficiently learned in a scenario where both the input states to the unitary and the measurements at the end can be chosen. The specific case of t=0t=0 has already been addressed in Ref. [81], and it would be interesting to generalize this to t>0t>0. Another promising direction is the study of the resource theory of fermionic non-Gaussianity, where the notion of Gaussian-nullity we introduced may play a significant role, similar to stabilizer nullity in the Clifford context [63, 64]. Finally, an analytical justification of the approximate tt-compressibility of impurity model dynamics remains an intriguing open problem, which we intend to explore in future research.

Supplementary Material II: Preliminaries

II.1 Notation and basics

In this work, we employ the following notation. ℒ⁡(ℂd)\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{C}^{d}) denotes the set of linear operators acting on the dd-dimensional complex vector space ℂd\mathbb{C}^{d}. Additionally, we use [d][d] to represent the set of integers from 1 to dd, i.e., [d]≔{1,…,d}[d]\coloneqq\{1,\dots,d\}. We denote with Mat⁡(d,𝔽)\mathrm{Mat}(d,\mathbb{F}) the set of d×dd\times d matrices over the field 𝔽\mathbb{F}. Let v∈ℂdv\in\mathbb{C}^{d} be a vector, and let p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty]. The pp-norm of vv is denoted by ‖v‖p\norm{v}_{p}, defined as ‖v‖p≔(∑i=1d|vi|p)1/p\norm{v}_{p}\coloneqq(\sum_{i=1}^{d}|v_{i}|^{p})^{1/p}. The Schatten pp-norm of a matrix A∈ℂdA\in\mathbb{C}^{d}, with p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty], is given by ‖A‖p≔Tr⁡((A†​A)p)1/p\norm{A}_{p}\coloneqq\Tr((\sqrt{A^\dagger A})^p)^{1/p}, corresponding to the pp-norm of the vector of singular values of AA. The trace norm and the Hilbert-Schmidt norm are important instances of Schatten pp-norms, denoted as ‖⋅‖1\norm{\cdot}_{1} and ‖⋅‖2\norm{\cdot}_{2} respectively. The Hilbert-Schmidt norm is induced by the Hilbert-Schmidt scalar product ⟨A,B⟩H​S≔Tr⁡(A†​B)\langle A,B\rangle_{HS}\coloneqq\Tr(A^\dagger B) for A,B∈ℒ⁡(ℂd)A,B\in\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{C}^{d}). The infinity norm, ‖⋅‖∞\norm{\cdot}_{\infty}, of a matrix is defined as its largest singular value. This norm can be interpreted as the limit of the Schatten pp-norm of the matrix as pp approaches infinity. For any unitaries UU and VV, and a matrix AA, we have the unitary invariance property ‖U​A​V‖p=‖A‖p\norm{UAV}_{p}=\norm{A}_{p}. Also, ‖A⊗B‖p=‖A‖p​‖B‖p\norm{A\otimes B}_{p}=\norm{A}_{p}\norm{B}_{p} for A,B∈ℒ⁡(ℂd)A,B\in\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{C}^{d}). We denote with U⁡(n)\mathrm{U}(n) the group of n×nn\times n unitary matrices. We denote O⁡(2​n)\mathrm{O}(2n) as the group of real orthogonal 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n matrices. Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R}) denotes the group of symplectic matrices over the real field, defined as

Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)≔{S∈Mat⁡(2​n,ℝ):S​Ω​ST=Ω},\displaystyle\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})\coloneqq\{S\in\mathrm{Mat}(2n,\mathbb{R})\,:\,S\Omega S^{T}=\Omega\}, (S1)

where Ω≔⨁i=1n(01−10)\Omega\coloneqq\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}. The nn-qubits Pauli operators are represented as elements of the set {I,X,Y,Z}⊗n\{I,X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n}, where I,X,Y,ZI,X,Y,Z represent the standard single qubit Pauli. Pauli operators are traceless, Hermitian, they square to the identity, and form an orthogonal basis with respect to the Hilbert-Schmidt scalar product for the space of linear operators. We define the set of quantum states as 𝒮(ℂd)≔{ρ∈ℒ(ℂd):ρ≥0,Tr⁡(ρ)=1}\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{C}^{d})\coloneqq\{\rho\in\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{C}^{d}):\rho\geq 0,\,\Tr(\rho)=1\}. The trace distance between two quantum states ρ,σ\rho,\sigma is defined as dtr​(ρ,σ)≔12​‖ρ−σ‖1d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho,\sigma)\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\norm{\rho-\sigma}_{1}. For a function f⁡(n)f(n), if there exists a constant cc and a specific input size n0n_{0} such that f⁡(n)≤c⋅g⁡(n)f(n)\leq c\cdot g(n) for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, where g⁡(n)g(n) is a well-defined function, then we express it as f⁡(n)=𝒪⁡(g⁡(n))f(n)=\mathcal{O}(g(n)). This notation signifies the upper limit of how fast a function grows in relation to g⁡(n)g(n).

For a function f⁡(n)f(n), if there exists a constant cc and a specific input size n0n_{0} such that f⁡(n)≥c⋅g⁡(n)f(n)\geq c\cdot g(n) for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, where g⁡(n)g(n) is a well-defined function, then we express it as f⁡(n)=Ω⁡(g⁡(n))f(n)=\Omega(g(n)). This notation signifies the lower limit of how fast a function grows in relation to g⁡(n)g(n).

For a function f⁡(n)f(n), if for any constant cc, there exists an input size n0n_{0} such that f⁡(n)>c⋅g⁡(n)f(n)>c\cdot g(n) for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, where g⁡(n)g(n) is a well-defined function, then then we express it as f⁡(n)=ω⁡(g⁡(n))f(n)=\omega(g(n)). This notation implies that the function grows strictly faster than the provided lower bound.

II.2 Basics of probability theory

In this section, we present fundamental results from probability theory useful in our work.

Lemma 6 (Union bound).

Let A1,A2,…,AMA_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{M} be events in a probability space. The probability of the union of these events is bounded by the sum of their individual probabilities:

Pr⁡(⋃i=1MAi)≤∑i=1MPr⁡(Ai).\operatorname{Pr}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{M}A_{i}\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{M}\operatorname{Pr}(A_{i}).
Lemma 7 (Chernoff bound).

Consider a set of independent and identically distributed random variables {Xi}i=1N\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} with binary outcomes, taking values in {0,1}\{0,1\}. Define X≔∑i=1NXiX\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i} and μ≔𝔼⁡[X]\mu\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[X]. For any α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), the probability of XX being less than (1−α)(1-\alpha) times its expected value is exponentially bounded as follows:

Pr[X≤(1−α)μ]≤exp(−α2​μ2).\operatorname{Pr}\left[X\leq(1-\alpha)\mu\right]\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{\alpha^{2}\mu}{2}\right).
Lemma 8 (Hoeffding’s inequality).

Let {Xi}i=1N\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} be independent and identically distributed (i.i.d) random variables with values in [a,b]⊆ℝ[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb{R}. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, the probability of the deviation of X^:=(∑i=1NXi)/N\hat{X}:=(\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i})/N from its expected value is exponentially bounded as follows:

Pr⁡(|1N​∑i=1NXi−𝔼⁡[X^]|≥ε)≤2​exp⁡(−2​N​ε2(b−a)2).\operatorname{Pr}\!\left(\left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\hat{X}]\right|\geq\varepsilon\right)\leq 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{2N\varepsilon^{2}}{(b-a)^{2}}\right).
Corollary 9.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and δ>0\delta>0, let {Xi}i=1N\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} be i.i.d. random variables with values in [a,b]⊆ℝ[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb{R} and X^:=(∑i=1NXi)/N\hat{X}:=(\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i})/N. According to Hoeffding’s inequality, a sample size NN satisfying

N≥(b−a)22​ε2​log⁡(2δ)N\geq\frac{(b-a)^{2}}{2\varepsilon^{2}}\log\!\left(\frac{2}{\delta}\right)

suffices to guarantee that |1N​∑i=1NXi−𝔼⁡[X^]|<ε|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\hat{X}]|<\varepsilon with a probability of at least 1−δ1-\delta.

II.3 Fermionic Gaussian states

In this section, we explore the definitions and essential properties of fermionic Gaussian states. We focus on a system consisting of nn qubits or nn fermionic modes, resulting in a Hilbert space dimension of 2n2^{n}. More precisely, our work is approached from two perspectives: examining a system of nn qubits with 1D matchgates circuits and their magic gates (e.g., SWAP gates), or an equivalent native fermionic system of nn modes with states prepared by fermionic Gaussian evolutions and local non-Gaussian evolutions. These perspectives are mathematically connected through the Jordan-Wigner mapping, which we use now for defining Majorana operators in terms of Pauli operators.

Definition 10 (Majorana operators).

For each k∈[n]k\in\left[n\right], Majorana operators are defined as:

γ2​k−1≔(∏j=1k−1Zj)​Xk,γ2​k≔(∏j=1k−1Zj)​Yk.\displaystyle\gamma_{2k-1}\coloneqq\left(\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}Z_{j}\right)X_{k},\quad\gamma_{2k}\coloneqq\left(\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}Z_{j}\right)Y_{k}. (S2)

Majorana operators can also be defined directly in the fermionic language through their anticommutation relations [15, 57]. Majorana operators are Hermitian, traceless, and their squares yield the identity, as deducible from their definitions. Moreover, distinct Majorana operators exhibit anticommutativity and orthogonality with respect to the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product.

Definition 11 (Majorana ordered products).

Given a set S≔{μ1,…,μ|S|}⊆[2​n]S\coloneqq\{\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{|S|}\}\subseteq[2n] with 1≤μ1<⋯<μ|S|≤2​n1\leq\mu_{1}<\dots<\mu_{|S|}\leq 2n, we define the Majorana product operator as γS=γμ1⋯γμ|S|\gamma_{S}=\gamma_{\mu_{1}}\cdots\gamma_{\mu_{|S|}} if S≠∅S\neq\emptyset, and γ∅=I\gamma_{\emptyset}=I otherwise.

The 4n4^{n} distinct ordered Majorana products are orthogonal to each other with respect the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product, therefore they form a basis for the linear operators ℒ⁡(ℂ2n)\mathcal{L}\!\left(\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}}\right).

Definition 12 (Fermionic Gaussian Unitary (FGU)).

A fermionic Gaussian unitary GOG_{O} is a unitary operator satisfying:

GO†​γμ​GO=∑ν=12​nOμ,ν​γν\displaystyle G^{\dagger}_{O}\gamma_{\mu}G_{O}=\sum^{2n}_{\nu=1}O_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_{\nu} (S3)

for any μ∈[2​n]\mu\in[2n], where O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n) is an orthogonal matrix.

Since the ordered products of Majorana operators γμ\gamma_{\mu} with μ∈[2​n]\mu\in[2n] form a basis for the linear operators, it is sufficient to specify how a unitary acts under conjugation on the 2​n2n Majorana operators γμ\gamma_{\mu}, where μ∈[2​n]\mu\in[2n], to uniquely determine the unitary up to a phase. Thus, there is a one-to-one mapping between nn-qubit fermionic Gaussian unitaries (up to a global phase) and orthogonal matrices O⁡(2​n)\mathrm{O}(2n). In particular, given O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n), it is possible to build the associated unitary using at most 𝒪⁡(n⁡(n−1)/2)\mathcal{O}(n(n-1)/2) 22-qubit FGU operations. For a more detailed explanation on how to map an O⁡(2​n)\mathrm{O}(2n) matrix to a fermionic Gaussian unitary, refer to [38, 58, 82]. From the previous definition, it readily follows that GO†=GOTG^{\dagger}_{O}=G_{O^{T}}. Moreover we have that the product of two Gaussian unitaries is Gaussian, namely (GO1​GO2)†​γμ​GO1​GO2=∑ν=12​n(O1​O2)μ,ν​γν(G_{O_{1}}G_{O_{2}})^{\dagger}\gamma_{\mu}G_{O_{1}}G_{O_{2}}=\sum^{2n}_{\nu=1}(O_{1}O_{2})_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_{\nu}. To streamline notation, we will frequently refer to fermionic Gaussian unitaries GOG_{O} simply as GG when there is no need to specify the associated orthogonal matrix. Now, we define a fermionic Gaussian state.

Definition 13 (Fermionic Gaussian state).

An nn-qubit state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is a (pure) fermionic Gaussian state if it can be expressed as |ψ⟩=G​|0n⟩\ket{\psi}=G\ket{0^n}, where GG is a fermionic Gaussian unitary.

It is noteworthy that any computational basis state |x⟩\ket{x} is a Gaussian state. This stems from the observation that each Pauli XiX_{i} gate acting on the ii-th qubit, where i∈[n]i\in[n], is a fermionic Gaussian unitary. An additional useful identity is Zj=−i​γ2​j−1​γ2​jZ_{j}=-i\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}. Thus, the density matrix of a pure fermionic Gaussian state associated to an orthogonal matrix O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n) can be written as:

GO​|0n⟩⟨0n|​GO†=GO​(∏j=1nI−i​γ2​j−1​γ2​j2)​GO†=∏j=1n(I−i​γ~2​j−1​γ~2​j2),\displaystyle G_{O}\outerproduct{0^n}{0^n}G_{O}^{\dagger}=G_{O}\left(\prod^{n}_{j=1}\frac{I-i\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}}{2}\right)G_{O}^{\dagger}=\prod^{n}_{j=1}\left(\frac{I-i\tilde{\gamma}_{2j-1}\tilde{\gamma}_{2j}}{2}\right), (S4)

where γ~μ:=GO​γμ​GO†=∑ν=12​nOμ,νT​γν\tilde{\gamma}_{\mu}:=G_{O}\gamma_{\mu}G^{{\dagger}}_{O}=\sum^{2n}_{\nu=1}O^{T}_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_{\nu} for each μ∈[2​n]\mu\in[2n].

It can be shown that free-fermionic Hamiltonians, which are quadratic Hamiltonians in the Majorana operators, i.e., Hfree≔i​∑p,q=12​nhp,q​γp​γqH_{\mathrm{free}}\coloneqq i\sum_{p,q=1}^{2n}h_{p,q}\gamma_{p}\gamma_{q}, where hh is a real anti-symmetric matrix, have fermionic Gaussian states as their ground states. Moreover, it can be shown that their time evolutions are fermionic Gaussian unitaries.

We now proceed to define the correlation matrix for any (possibly non-Gaussian) state.

Definition 14 (Correlation Matrix).

For any nn-qubit quantum state ρ\rho, its correlation matrix C⁡(ρ)C(\rho) is defined as:

[C⁡(ρ)]j,k≔−i2​Tr⁡([γj,γk]​ρ),\displaystyle[C(\rho)]_{j,k}\coloneqq-\frac{i}{2}\Tr\left(\left[\gamma_{j},\gamma_{k}\right]\rho\right), (S5)

where j,k∈[2​n].j,k\in[2n].

The correlation matrix of any state is real and anti-symmetric, possessing eigenvalues in pairs ±i​λj\pm i\lambda_{j} for j∈[2​n]j\in[2n], where λj\lambda_{j} are real numbers such that |λj|≤1|\lambda_{j}|\leq 1. The correlation matrix of a quantum state, when evolved using fermionic Gaussian unitaries, undergoes a transformation through conjugation with the corresponding orthogonal matrix, as articulated in the following lemma.

Lemma 15 (Transformation of the Correlation Matrix under FGU).

For a given nn-qubit state ρ\rho, we have:

C⁡(GO​ρ​GO†)=O​C​(ρ)​OT,\displaystyle C(G_{O}\rho G_{O}^{\dagger})=OC(\rho)O^{T}, (S6)

for any orthogonal matrix O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n) and associated fermionic Gaussian unitary GOG_{O}.

This result is readily verified through the definitions of the correlation matrix and fermionic Gaussian unitary. The state |x⟩\ket{x} is characterized by a correlation matrix of the form:

C⁡(|x⟩⟨x|)=⨁j=1n(0(−1)xi−(−1)xi0).\displaystyle C(\outerproduct{x}{x})=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}0&(-1)^{x_{i}}\\ -(-1)^{x_{i}}&0\end{pmatrix}. (S7)

Hence, for a fermionic Gaussian state |ψ⟩≔GO​|0n⟩\ket{\psi}\coloneqq G_{O}\ket{0^n}, the correlation matrix takes the form:

C⁡(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|)=O​⨁j=1n(01−10)​OT.\displaystyle C(\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi})=O\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}O^{T}. (S8)

In the subsequent discussion, we will use C⁡(|ψ⟩)C(\ket{\psi}) to denote the correlation matrix of a pure state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}. If the state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is a pure Gaussian state, then each of the eigenvalues of C⁡(|ψ⟩)C(\ket{\psi}) is one in absolute value. Moreover, it is worth noting that every real anti-symmetric matrix can be decomposed in the following form:

Lemma 16 (Normal form of real anti-symmetric matrices [60]).

Any real anti-symmetric matrix CC can be decomposed in the so-called ‘normal-form’:

C=O​⨁j=1n(0λj−λj0)​OT,\displaystyle C=O\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}0&\lambda_{j}\\ -\lambda_{j}&0\end{pmatrix}O^{T}, (S9)

where OO is an orthogonal matrix in O⁡(2​n)\mathrm{O}(2n) and λj≥0∈ℝ\lambda_{j}\geq 0\in\mathbb{R}, for any j∈[n]j\in[n], are ordered in increasing order. The eigenvalues of CC are ±i​λj\pm i\lambda_{j} where λj∈ℝ\lambda_{j}\in\mathbb{R} for any j∈[n]j\in[n].

Definition 17 (Normal eigenvalues).

Given a real-antisymmetric matrix decomposed as in the previous Lemma 16, {λj}j=1n\{\lambda_{j}\}^{n}_{j=1} are dubbed as the ‘normal eigenvalues’ of the matrix.

II.4 Particle-number preserving unitaries

In this section, we introduce the concept of particle-number preserving fermionic unitaries and establish definitions and facts useful for subsequent discussions. We begin by defining creation and annihilation operators.

Definition 18 (Creation and annihilation operators).

The annihilation operators are defined as:

aj≔γ2​j−1+i​γ2​j2,\displaystyle a_{j}\coloneqq\frac{\gamma_{2j-1}+i\gamma_{2j}}{2}, (S10)

for any j∈[n]j\in[n]. The creation operators {aj†}j=1n\{a^{\dagger}_{j}\}^{n}_{j=1} are defined as the adjoints of the annihilation operators.

Definition 19 (Particle number operator).

The operator N^≔∑i=1nai†​ai\hat{N}\coloneqq\sum^{n}_{i=1}a^{{\dagger}}_{i}a_{i} is denoted as the particle number operator.

The computational basis forms a set of eigenstates for the particle number operator:

N^​|x1,…,xn⟩=(x1+⋯+xn)​|x1,…,xn⟩,\displaystyle\hat{N}\ket{x_1,\dots, x_n}=(x_{1}+\dots+x_{n})\ket{x_1,\dots,x_n}, (S11)

where x1,…,xn∈{0,1}x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\{0,1\}.

Definition 20 (Particle number preserving unitaries).

A unitary UU is said to be particle number preserving if and only if

U†​N^​U=N^,\displaystyle U^{{\dagger}}\hat{N}U=\hat{N}, (S12)

where N^≔∑i=1nai†​ai\hat{N}\coloneqq\sum^{n}_{i=1}a^{{\dagger}}_{i}a_{i} is the particle number operator.

Definition 21 (Symplectic group).

The group of real symplectic matrices, denoted as Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R}), is defined as

Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)≔{S∈Mat⁡(2​n,ℝ):S​Ω​ST=Ω},\displaystyle\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})\coloneqq\{S\in\mathrm{Mat}(2n,\mathbb{R})\,:\,S\Omega S^{T}=\Omega\}, (S13)

where Ω≔⨁i=1n(01−10)=⨁i=1ni​Y\Omega\coloneqq\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}iY.

It is often convenient to express Ω\Omega as Ω=In⊗i​Y\Omega=I_{n}\otimes iY, where InI_{n} denotes the n×nn\times n identity matrix. Note that Ω\Omega in the literature is sometimes defined (see, e.g., [61]) as i​Y⊗In=(0nIn−In0n)iY\otimes I_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}0_{n}&I_{n}\\ -I_{n}&0_{n}\end{pmatrix}, but the two definitions are equivalent up to orthogonal transformation.

Now, we state an important proposition that will be useful in the subsequent section.

Proposition 22 (U⁡(n)\mathrm{U}(n) is isomorphic to O⁡(2​n)∩Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)\mathrm{O}(2n)\cap\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})).

The set of unitaries U⁡(n)\mathrm{U}(n) is isomorphic to the set of real symplectic orthogonal matrices O⁡(2​n)∩Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)\mathrm{O}(2n)\cap\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R}).

In particular, any orthogonal symplectic matrix O∈O⁡(2​n)∩Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n)\cap\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R}) can be written as follows:

O=Re(u)⊗I+Im(u)⊗iY,\displaystyle O=\real(u)\otimes I+\imaginary(u)\otimes iY, (S14)

where u∈U⁡(n)u\in\mathrm{U}(n) is an n×nn\times n unitary.

Proof.

We refer the reader to Appendix B.1 of the book [61] for a detailed proof. However, by inspection, it can be verified that the matrix OO defined in this way is both orthogonal and symplectic. This follows from the unitarity of uu, which implies the relations:

Re(u)Re(u)t+Im(u)Im(u)t=I,Re(u)Im(u)t−Im(u)Re(u)t=0.\displaystyle\real(u)\real(u)^{t}+\imaginary(u)\imaginary(u)^{t}=I,\quad\quad\real(u)\imaginary(u)^{t}-\imaginary(u)\real(u)^{t}=0. (S15)

∎

We now present a Lemma, which shows (some) equivalent definitions of a particle-number preserving fermionic Gaussian unitary.

Lemma 23 (Particle number preserving Gaussian unitary).

Let GG be a fermionic Gaussian unitary associated with the orthogonal matrix O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n). The following points are equivalents:

  1. 1.

    GG is particle number-preserving,

  2. 2.

    G​|0n⟩⟨0n|​G†=|0n⟩⟨0n|G\outerproduct{0^n}{0^n}G^{{\dagger}}=\outerproduct{0^n}{0^n},

  3. 3.

    OO is symplectic orthogonal, i.e., O∈O⁡(2​n)∩Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n)\cap\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R}).

Proof.

If GG is particle number-preserving, then

G†​N^​G​|0n⟩=N^​|0n⟩=0,\displaystyle G^{{\dagger}}\hat{N}G\ket{0^n}=\hat{N}\ket{0^n}=0, (S16)

where the first equality uses Definition 20. This implies N^​G​|0n⟩=0\hat{N}G\ket{0^n}=0. Since the ground space corresponding to the zero eigenvalue of the particle number operator N^\hat{N} is one-dimensional and spanned by |0n⟩\ket{0^n}, it follows that G​|0n⟩G\ket{0^n} is equal to |0n⟩\ket{0^n}, up to a phase. Thus, 1. implies 2.

Noting that |0n⟩⟨0n|\outerproduct{0^n}{0^n} is a Gaussian state with a correlation matrix Ω=⨁j=1ni​Y\Omega=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}iY, we deduce that the correlation matrix of G​|0n⟩⟨0n|​G†G\outerproduct{0^n}{0^n}G^{\dagger} is O​Ω​OTO\Omega O^{T}. Therefore the condition G​|0n⟩⟨0n|​G†=|0n⟩⟨0n|G\outerproduct{0^n}{0^n}G^{{\dagger}}=\outerproduct{0^n}{0^n} is equivalent to O​Ω​OT=ΩO\Omega O^{T}=\Omega, i.e., OO is a real symplectic orthogonal matrix. This proves that 2. is equivalent to 3.

Now, let us assume that O∈O⁡(2​n)∩Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n)\cap\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R}). Then, we have for l∈[n]l\in[n]:

G†​al​G\displaystyle G^{{\dagger}}a_{l}G =G†​(γ2​l−1+i​γ2​l2)​G=∑j=12​n(O2​l−1,j+i​O2​l,j)​γj2\displaystyle=G^{{\dagger}}\left(\frac{\gamma_{2l-1}+i\gamma_{2l}}{2}\right)G=\sum^{2n}_{j=1}\left(O_{2l-1,j}+iO_{2l,j}\right)\frac{\gamma_{j}}{2} (S17)
=∑j=1n(O2​l−1,2​j−1+i​O2​l,2​j−1)​γ2​j−12+∑j=1n(O2​l−1,2​j+i​O2​l,2​j)​γ2​j2,\displaystyle=\sum^{n}_{j=1}\left(O_{2l-1,2j-1}+iO_{2l,2j-1}\right)\frac{\gamma_{2j-1}}{2}+\sum^{n}_{j=1}\left(O_{2l-1,2j}+iO_{2l,2j}\right)\frac{\gamma_{2j}}{2}, (S18)
=∑j=1n(Re(u)l,j+iIm(u)l,j)γ2​j−12+∑j=1n(−Im(u)l,j+iRe(u)l,j)γ2​j2,\displaystyle=\sum^{n}_{j=1}\left(\real(u)_{l,j}+i\imaginary(u)_{l,j}\right)\frac{\gamma_{2j-1}}{2}+\sum^{n}_{j=1}\left(-\imaginary(u)_{l,j}+i\real(u)_{l,j}\right)\frac{\gamma_{2j}}{2}, (S19)
=∑j=1nul,j​(γ2​j−1+i​γ2​j)2=∑j=1nul,j​aj.\displaystyle=\sum^{n}_{j=1}u_{l,j}\frac{\left(\gamma_{2j-1}+i\gamma_{2j}\right)}{2}=\sum^{n}_{j=1}u_{l,j}a_{j}. (S20)

where in the fourth equality we used that O∈O⁡(2​n)∩Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n)\cap\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R}), and so, because of Proposition 22, it can be written as O=Re(u)⊗I+Im(u)⊗iYO=\real(u)\otimes I+\imaginary(u)\otimes iY where u∈U⁡(n)u\in\mathrm{U}(n) is a n×nn\times n unitary. Similarly, we have G†​al†​G=∑j=1nul,j∗​aj†G^{{\dagger}}a^{{\dagger}}_{l}G=\sum^{n}_{j=1}u^{*}_{l,j}a^{{\dagger}}_{j}. This implies

G†​N^​G=∑l=1nG†​al†​al​G=∑l,j,k=1nul,j∗​ul,k​aj†​ak=∑j=1naj†​aj=N^,\displaystyle G^{{\dagger}}\hat{N}G=\sum^{n}_{l=1}G^{{\dagger}}a^{\dagger}_{l}a_{l}G=\sum^{n}_{l,j,k=1}u^{*}_{l,j}u_{l,k}a^{{\dagger}}_{j}a_{k}=\sum^{n}_{j=1}a^{\dagger}_{j}a_{j}=\hat{N}, (S21)

where we used the unitarity of uu in the last step. This proves that 3. implies 1. ∎

Supplementary Material III: Structure of tt-doped Gaussian unitaries and states

In this section, we analyze the concept of tt-doped fermionic Gaussian unitaries and states.

Definition 24 (tt-doped fermionic Gaussian unitary).

A unitary UtU_{t} is a (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped fermionic Gaussian unitary if it can be decomposed in terms of Gaussian unitaries {Gi}i=0t\{G_{i}\}^{t}_{i=0} and at most tt non-Gaussian κ\kappa-local gates {Wi}i=1t\{W_{i}\}^{t}_{i=1}, specifically

Ut=GtWt⋯G1W1G0.\displaystyle U_{t}=G_{t}W_{t}\cdots G_{1}W_{1}G_{0}. (S22)

Here κ\kappa-local refers to the number of distinct Majorana operators that generate each non-Gaussian gate. Informally, a unitary is tt-doped Gaussian if it is (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped Gaussian for some fixed constant κ\kappa.

In our work, we consider non-Gaussian gates Wt′W_{t^{\prime}} for t′∈[t]t^{\prime}\in[t], each generated by κ≤2​n\kappa\leq 2n in κ\kappa fixed Majorana operators {γμ⁡(t′,j)}j=1κ\{\gamma_{\mu(t^{\prime},j)}\}^{\kappa}_{j=1}, where μ⁡(t′,1),…,μ⁡(t′,κ)∈[2​n]\mu(t^{\prime},1),\dots,\mu(t^{\prime},\kappa)\in[2n]. For κ=3\kappa=3, an example of a non-Gaussian gate is exp⁡(θ​γ1​γ2​γ3)=exp⁡(−i​Y1​θ)\exp(\theta\gamma_1 \gamma_2 \gamma_3)=\exp(-i Y_1\theta), where θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R}, and for κ=4\kappa=4, an example is the SWAP\operatorname{SWAP}-gate.

Definition 25 (tt-doped fermionic Gaussian state).

An nn-qubit state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is a (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped (informally, tt-doped) fermionic Gaussian state if it can be expressed as |ψ⟩=Ut​|0n⟩\ket{\psi}=U_{t}\ket{0^n}, where UtU_{t} is a (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped (tt-doped) fermionic Gaussian unitary.

III.1 Compression of tt-doped Gaussian unitaries and states

We start by presenting a Theorem which shows how all non-Gaussianity in a tt-doped unitary can be ‘compressed’ or ‘moved’ to the first few qubits.

Theorem 26 (Compression of non-Gaussianity in tt-doped unitaries).

Any (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped fermionic Gaussian unitary UtU_{t} can be expressed as:

Ut=GA​(ut⊗I)​GB,\displaystyle U_{t}=G_{A}(u_{t}\otimes I)G_{B}, (S23)

where GAG_{A}, GBG_{B} are Gaussian unitaries, and utu_{t} is a unitary supported exclusively on ⌈κ​t2⌉\lceil\frac{\kappa t}{2}\rceil qubits.

Proof.

Let us denote M≔κ​tM\coloneqq\kappa t. We express the tt-doped unitary as Ut=(∏t′=1tGt′​Wt′)​G0U_{t}=(\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}G_{t^{\prime}}W_{t^{\prime}})G_{0}. Rearranging it, we have

Ut=G~t​∏t′=1tW~t′,\displaystyle U_{t}=\tilde{G}_{t}\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}, (S24)

where W~t′≔G~t′−1†​Wt′​G~t′−1\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}\coloneqq\tilde{G}^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}-1}W_{t^{\prime}}\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}-1} and G~t′≔Gt′..G0\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}}\coloneqq G_{t^{\prime}}..G_{0}. Informally, the idea behind this rewriting is that Gaussian operations act nicely under conjugation. Next, we rewrite

Ut=G~t​Gaux​∏t′=1t(Gaux†​W~t′​Gaux)​Gaux†,\displaystyle U_{t}=\tilde{G}_{t}G_{\mathrm{aux}}\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}(G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}G_{\mathrm{aux}})G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}, (S25)

by introducing a Gaussian operation GauxG_{\mathrm{aux}} that we fix later and that will be responsible for moving all the non-Gaussian gates to the first qubits. Now, we set:

GA\displaystyle G_{A} ≔G~t​Gaux\displaystyle\coloneqq\tilde{G}_{t}G_{\mathrm{aux}} (S26)
ut\displaystyle u_{t} ≔∏t′=1t(Gaux†​W~t′​Gaux)\displaystyle\coloneqq\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}(G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}G_{\mathrm{aux}}) (S27)
GB\displaystyle G_{B} ≔Gaux†.\displaystyle\coloneqq G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}. (S28)

Note that GAG_{A} so-defined is Gaussian because the product of Gaussian unitaries is Gaussian, and GBG_{B} is clearly Gaussian because the adjoint of a Gaussian unitary is Gaussian. We need to show that it is possible to choose GauxG_{\mathrm{aux}} such that utu_{t} is supported only on the first ⌈M/2⌉\lceil M/2\rceil qubits.

More precisely, we will require that GauxG_{\mathrm{aux}} ensures that each Gaux†​W~t′​GauxG^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}G_{\mathrm{aux}} is generated by the first MM Majorana operators alone. We will achieve it by ensuring that the Heisenberg evolution under G~t′−1​Gaux\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}-1}G_{\mathrm{aux}}, of each Majorana that generates Wt′W_{t^{\prime}}, has non-trivial support exclusively on the first MM Majorana operators. To find GauxG_{\mathrm{aux}} with the desired property, we will find the associated orthogonal matrix OauxO_{\mathrm{aux}}. Let {μ⁡(t′,r)}t′∈[t],r∈[κ]\{\mu(t^{\prime},r)\}_{t^{\prime}\in[t],r\in[\kappa]}, with μ⁡(t′,r)∈[2​n]\mu(t^{\prime},r)\in[2n], be the set of indices of Majorana operators generating the t′t^{\prime}-th non-Gaussian gate (listed in increasing order). For example, consider κ=4\kappa=4 and the t′t^{\prime}-th non-Gaussian gate Wt′≔exp⁡(i​γ2​γ4​γ6​γ9+i​γ4)W_{t^{\prime}}\coloneqq\exp\!\left(i\gamma_{2}\gamma_{4}\gamma_{6}\gamma_{9}+i\gamma_{4}\right). In this case, μ⁡(t′,3)=6\mu{(t^{\prime},3)}=6. For each such Majorana operator γμ⁡(t′,r)\gamma_{\mu(t^{\prime},r)}, where r∈[2​n]r\in[2n], its Heisenberg evolution yields

Gaux†​G~t′−1†​γμ⁡(t′,r)​G~t′−1​Gaux=∑m=12​n(Ot′−1​Oaux)μ⁡(t′,r),m​γm,\displaystyle G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{G}^{{\dagger}}_{t^{\prime}-1}\gamma_{\mu(t^{\prime},r)}\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}-1}G_{\mathrm{aux}}=\sum^{2n}_{m=1}(O_{t^{\prime}-1}O_{\mathrm{aux}})_{\mu(t^{\prime},r),m}\gamma_{m}, (S29)

where Ot′−1O_{t^{\prime}-1} is the orthogonal matrix associated with G~t′−1\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}-1}. Our demand on the support of Heisenberg-evolved γμ⁡(t′,r)\gamma_{\mu(t^{\prime},r)} implies

(Ot′−1​Oaux)μ⁡(t′,r),m=(OauxT​Ot′−1T)m,μ⁡(t′,r)=0\displaystyle(O_{t^{\prime}-1}O_{\mathrm{aux}})_{\mu(t^{\prime},r),m}=(O^{T}_{\mathrm{aux}}O^{T}_{t^{\prime}-1})_{m,\mu(t^{\prime},r)}=0 (S30)

for any m∈{M+1,…,2​n}m\in\{M+1,\dots,2n\}.

Let us denote as {𝐞i}i=12​n\{\mathbf{e}_{i}\}^{2n}_{i=1} the canonical basis vectors of ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n}. For easy notation, we now denote the unit norm vectors {Ot′−1T​𝐞μ⁡(t′,r)}t′∈[t],r∈[κ]\{O^{T}_{t^{\prime}-1}\mathbf{e}_{{\mu(t^{\prime},r)}}\}_{t^{\prime}\in[t],r\in[\kappa]} with the set of vectors {𝐯j}j=1M\{\mathbf{v}_{j}\}^{M}_{j=1} (remember that M=κ​tM=\kappa t). We can prove the existence of such OauxO_{\mathrm{aux}} by proving the existence of its transpose O≔OauxTO\coloneqq O^{T}_{\mathrm{aux}}. In such notation, the condition in Eq.(S30) reads as:

𝐞mT​O​𝐯j=0,\displaystyle\mathbf{e}^{T}_{m}O\mathbf{v}_{j}=0, (S31)

for any j∈[M]j\in[M] and m∈{M+1,…,2​n}m\in\{M+1,\dots,2n\}. In other words, we need to prove the existence of an orthogonal matrix OO that maps any given real vectors 𝐯1,…,𝐯M∈ℝ2​n\mathbf{v}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}, where M≤2​nM\leq 2n, to the span of the first MM canonical basis vectors of ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n}. The existence of such a matrix is readily established by selecting an orthonormal basis for W≔Span⁡(𝐯1,…,𝐯M)W\coloneqq\operatorname{Span}(\mathbf{v}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_{M}) and defining the orthogonal matrix that maps this orthonormal basis to the first dim⁡(W)≤M\operatorname{dim}(W)\leq M canonical basis vectors. This concludes the proof. ∎

The subsequent Theorem 27 demonstrates the compression of tt-doped Gaussian states.

Theorem 27 (Compression of non-Gaussianity in tt-doped Gaussian states).

Any (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped fermionic Gaussian state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} can be represented as:

|ψ⟩=G⁡(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−κ​t⟩),\displaystyle\ket{\psi}=G(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-\kappa t}}), (S32)

where GG is a Gaussian unitary, and |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is a state supported exclusively on κ​t\kappa t qubits.

Proof.

Let |ψ⟩≔Ut​|0n⟩\ket{\psi}\coloneqq U_{t}\ket{0^n}, where Ut=(∏t′=1tGt′​Wt′)​G0U_{t}=(\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}G_{t^{\prime}}W_{t^{\prime}})G_{0} is a tt-doped fermionic Gaussian unitary. The proof begins analogously to the one of the previous Theorem 26 and it uses the same notation. In particular, we have:

Ut=G~t​Gaux​∏t′=1t(Gaux†​W~t′​Gaux)​Gaux†,\displaystyle U_{t}=\tilde{G}_{t}G_{\mathrm{aux}}\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}(G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}G_{\mathrm{aux}})G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}, (S33)

where W~t′≔G~t′−1†​Wt′​G~t′−1\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}\coloneqq\tilde{G}^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}-1}W_{t^{\prime}}\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}-1} and G~t′≔Gt′..G0\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}}\coloneqq G_{t^{\prime}}..G_{0}. We set, as before

GA\displaystyle G_{A} ≔G~t​Gaux\displaystyle\coloneqq\tilde{G}_{t}G_{\mathrm{aux}} (S34)
ut\displaystyle u_{t} ≔∏t′=1t(Gaux†​W~t′​Gaux)\displaystyle\coloneqq\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}(G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}G_{\mathrm{aux}}) (S35)
GB\displaystyle G_{B} ≔Gaux†.\displaystyle\coloneqq G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}. (S36)

However, now, we require that utu_{t} has support on the first MM qubits, where M≔κ​tM\coloneqq\kappa t (while in the previous proof of Theorem 26 we requested ⌈M/2⌉\lceil M/2\rceil), or, equivalently, we request that the generators of Gaux†​W~t′​GauxG^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{W}_{t^{\prime}}G_{\mathrm{aux}} for any t′∈[t]t^{\prime}\in[t] involve only the first 2​M2M Majorana operators.

This time we also impose that Gaux†​|0n⟩=|0n⟩G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\ket{0^n}=\ket{0^n}. This implies that OauxT∈Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)O^{T}_{\mathrm{aux}}\in\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R}) (where OauxO_{\mathrm{aux}} is the orthogonal matrix associated to GauxG_{\mathrm{aux}}), i.e. OauxTO^{T}_{\mathrm{aux}} must be a symplectic orthogonal matrix, because of Lemma 23. We now define O≔OauxTO\coloneqq O^{T}_{\mathrm{aux}}.

Similarly to the previous theorem and using the same notation, we can ensure that utu_{t} is supported only on the first MM qubits by demonstrating the existence of an orthogonal, but this time also symplectic, matrix OO that satisfies:

𝐞mT​O​𝐯j=0,\displaystyle\mathbf{e}^{T}_{m}O\mathbf{v}_{j}=0, (S37)

for any j∈[M]j\in[M] with arbitrary 𝐯1,…,𝐯M\mathbf{v}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_{M} real vectors, and m∈{2​M+1,…,2​n}m\in\{2M+1,\dots,2n\}. The existence of such OO follows from the subsequent Lemma 28, which crucially uses the isomorphism between 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n symplectic orthogonal real matrices and n×nn\times n unitaries [61]. ∎

Lemma 28 (Compression via symplectic orthogonal transformations).

Let {𝐞i}i=12​n\{\mathbf{e}_{i}\}^{2n}_{i=1} be the canonical basis of ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n}. Let 𝐯1,…,𝐯M∈ℝ2​n\mathbf{v}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n} be a set of unit-norm real vectors, where M≤nM\leq n. There exists an orthogonal symplectic matrix O∈O⁡(2​n)∩Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n)\cap\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R}) such that

𝐞iT​O​𝐯j=0,\displaystyle\mathbf{e}^{T}_{i}O\mathbf{v}_{j}=0, (S38)

for all i∈{2​M+1,…,2​n}i\in\{2M+1,\dots,2n\} and j∈[M]j\in[M], meaning that all {O​𝐯j}j=1M\{O\mathbf{v}_{j}\}^{M}_{j=1} are exclusively supported on the span of the first 2​M2M canonical basis vectors.

Proof.

Orthogonal symplectic matrices O∈O⁡(2​n)∩Sp⁡(2​n,ℝ)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n)\cap\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R}) have a bijective correspondence with unitary matrices U∈U⁡(n)U\in\mathrm{U}(n) through a well-defined vector space mapping [61] (see Proposition 22). Specifically, for a 2​n2n-dimensional real vector 𝐰≔(w1,…,w2​n)\mathbf{w}\coloneqq(w_{1},\dots,w_{2n}), there exists a bijective mapping to an nn-dimensional complex vector 𝐟⁡(𝐰)≔(w1−i​w2,…,w2​n−1−i​w2​n)\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{w})\coloneqq(w_{1}-iw_{2},\dots,w_{2n-1}-iw_{2n}). A unitary transformation UU in this nn-dimensional complex space corresponds to an orthogonal symplectic transformation OO in the corresponding 2​n2n-dimensional real space, and vice versa. Thus, finding a unitary UU that maps the span of 𝐟⁡(𝐯1),…,𝐟⁡(𝐯M)\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{v}_{1}),\dots,\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{v}_{M}) to the span of the first MM canonical basis vectors of this nn-dimensional complex space implies the existence of a symplectic orthogonal matrix OO that maps 𝐯1,…,𝐯M\mathbf{v}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_{M} to the span of the first 2​M2M canonical basis vectors of the 2​n2n-dimensional real space. To establish the existence of such a unitary, consider the complex vector subspace W≔Span⁡(𝐟⁡(𝐯1),…,𝐟⁡(𝐯M))W\coloneqq\operatorname{Span}(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{v}_{1}),\dots,\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{v}_{M})) of dimension at most MM. By selecting an orthonormal basis for this subspace, we can construct a unitary matrix UU that maps this basis to the first dim⁡(W)≤M\mathrm{dim}(W)\leq M canonical basis vectors. Hence, the existence of the required unitary matrix is confirmed, implying the existence of a symplectic orthogonal matrix OO that maps 𝐯1,…,𝐯M\mathbf{v}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_{M} to the span of the first 2​M2M canonical basis vectors. This concludes our proof. ∎

It is noteworthy that the ‘compressed size’ obtained for tt-doped unitaries, which is ⌈κ​t/2⌉\lceil\kappa t/2\rceil, is less than κ​t\kappa t which we proved for tt-doped Gaussian states.

III.2 Compression of tt-doped Gaussian particle-number preserving unitaries

The subsequent Proposition 29 demonstrates that the compression of tt-doped Gaussian unitaries can also be achieved in the particle-number preserving case.

Proposition 29 (Particle number preserving tt-doped unitaries).

Let UtU_{t} be a tt-doped fermionic Gaussian unitary, as per Definition 24, where all the unitaries that compose UtU_{t} are particle-number preserving. Then UtU_{t} can be decomposed as:

Ut≔GA​(ut⊗I)​GB,\displaystyle U_{t}\coloneqq G_{A}(u_{t}\otimes I)G_{B}, (S39)

where GAG_{A} and GBG_{B} are Gaussian unitaries which preserve the number of particles (see Definition 20) and utu_{t} is a particle-number preserving possibly non-Gaussian unitary supported on κ​t\kappa t qubits.

Proof.

The proof of such proposition follows the same lines as the one of Theorem 27. In fact, by inspecting the proof, it readily follows that the so-defined GAG_{A} is particle-number preserving. The fact that GBG_{B} and utu_{t} are particle-number preserving follows from the condition Gaux†​|0n⟩=|0n⟩G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\ket{0^n}=\ket{0^n}, where GB≔Gaux†G_{B}\coloneqq G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}} and by Lemma 23. ∎

III.3 Circuit complexity of tt-doped Gaussian unitaries and states

The circuit complexity of a unitary (state) is defined as the minimum number of 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1)-local gates needed for implementing the unitary (state). We will consider locality both in the qubit and in the fermionic sense; in the latter case it refers to the number of distinct Majorana operators that generate each non-Gaussian gate. Our subject of interest is the scaling of the complexity of a tt-doped unitary. Throughout this section, we assume κ=𝒪⁡(1)\kappa=\mathcal{O}(1) and let t=t⁡(n)t=t(n) change in some way with nn.
