By Definition 24, a tt-doped Gaussian unitary UtU_{t} can be written as Ut=GtWt⋯G1W1G0U_{t}=G_{t}W_{t}\cdots G_{1}W_{1}G_{0}, where {Gi}i=0t\{G_{i}\}^{t}_{i=0} are Gaussian unitaries and {Wi}i=1t\{W_{i}\}^{t}_{i=1} are, possibly non-Gaussian, κ\kappa-local fermionic gates. From this definition and using the fact that any Gaussian unitary can be decomposed as the product of ≤2​n​(2​n−1)/2\leq 2n(2n-1)/2 (fermionic) 22-local gates [38, 58, 59], the fermionic circuit complexity of tt-doped Gaussian unitaries is upper-bounded by 𝒪⁡(n2​t)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}t). The same can be shown for qubit circuit complexity (see below). But more importantly, we have proven earlier that a tt-doped Gaussian unitary can be decomposed as Ut=GA​(ut⊗I)​GBU_{t}=G_{A}(u_{t}\otimes I)G_{B}, where GA,GBG_{A},G_{B} are Gaussians and utu_{t} is a unitary on ⌈κ​t2⌉\lceil\frac{\kappa t}{2}\rceil qubits. In the following, we show that such decomposition reveals an improved upper bound on the circuit complexity of tt-doped Gaussian unitaries.

Proposition 30 (Circuit complexity of tt-doped Gaussian unitaries).

The circuit complexity 𝒞⁡(Ut)\mathcal{C}(U_{t}) of a tt-doped Gaussian unitary UtU_{t} is (both in the qubit and fermionic sense):

𝒞⁡(Ut)={𝒪⁡(n2+t3),if κ​t≤n𝒪⁡(n2​t),otherwise.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}(U_{t})=\begin{cases}\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+t^{3}),&\text{if $\kappa t\leq n$}\\ \mathcal{O}(n^{2}t),&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (S40)
Proof.

Let us assume that κ​t≤n\kappa t\leq n. Then, UtU_{t} can be written as Ut=GA​(ut⊗I)​GBU_{t}=G_{A}(u_{t}\otimes I)G_{B}, where GA,GBG_{A},G_{B} are Gaussians and utu_{t} is a unitary on ⌈κ​t2⌉\lceil\frac{\kappa t}{2}\rceil qubits. In fact, utu_{t} is itself a (t,κ)(t,\kappa)-doped Gaussian unitary on ⌈κ​t2⌉\lceil\frac{\kappa t}{2}\rceil qubits. It is not directly obvious, but will be shown momentarily; this will imply the desired circuit complexity 𝒪⁡(t3)\mathcal{O}(t^{3}). We recall our definitions used in the proof of Theorem 26. We have G~t′≔Gt′..G0\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}}\coloneqq G_{t^{\prime}}..G_{0} for t′∈[t]t^{\prime}\in[t] and a Gaussian unitary GauxG_{\mathrm{aux}}, and set

ut\displaystyle u_{t} ≔∏t′=1t(Gaux†​G~t′−1†​Wt′​G~t′−1​Gaux)=∏t′=1twt′,\displaystyle\coloneqq\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}(G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{G}^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}-1}W_{t^{\prime}}\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}-1}G_{\mathrm{aux}})=\prod^{t}_{t^{\prime}=1}w_{t^{\prime}}, (S41)

where we defined the unitaries wt′≔Gaux†​G~t′−1†​Wt′​G~t′−1​Gauxw_{t^{\prime}}\coloneqq G^{{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{aux}}\tilde{G}^{\dagger}_{t^{\prime}-1}W_{t^{\prime}}\tilde{G}_{t^{\prime}-1}G_{\mathrm{aux}} which act only on the first ⌈κ​t2⌉\lceil\frac{\kappa t}{2}\rceil qubits (equivalently, fermionic modes). We note that wt′w_{t^{\prime}} is generated by κ\kappa Majorana operator superpositions of form ∑i=1κ​t[𝐯~j]i​γi\sum^{\kappa t}_{i=1}[\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{j}]_{i}\gamma_{i}, j∈[κ⁡(t′−1)+1,κ​t′]j\in[\kappa(t^{\prime}-1)+1,\kappa t^{\prime}]; here 𝐯~j≔O​𝐯j\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{j}\coloneqq O\mathbf{v}_{j} (cf. notation OO and 𝐯j\mathbf{v}_{j} from the proof of Theorem 26). Hence, for each of these (non-local) non-Gaussian unitaries wt′w_{t^{\prime}}, we can find a Gaussian operation gt′g_{t^{\prime}} on the first ⌈κ​t2⌉\lceil\frac{\kappa t}{2}\rceil qubits whose associated orthogonal matrix rotates vectors 𝐯~j\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{j} into the span of the first κ\kappa basis vectors. As a result, we have wt′=gt′†​w~t′​gt′w_{t^{\prime}}=g_{t^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\tilde{w}_{t^{\prime}}g_{t^{\prime}}, where w~t′\tilde{w}_{t^{\prime}} is now a κ\kappa-local non-Gaussian unitary generated by the first κ\kappa Majorana operators. By implication, it is also a local qubit gate acting on the first ⌈κ2⌉\lceil\frac{\kappa}{2}\rceil qubits. From this it follows that the circuit complexity of each wt′w_{t^{\prime}} scales as that of a Gaussian gt′g_{t^{\prime}}. As gt′g_{t^{\prime}} acts on the first O⁡(t)O(t) qubits/fermionic modes, its circuit complexity is O⁡(t2)O(t^{2}) both in the qubit and the fermionic sense. Therefore, the circuit complexity of utu_{t} is t​𝒪​(t2)=𝒪⁡(t3)t\mathcal{O}(t^{2})=\mathcal{O}(t^{3}). Moreover, the circuit complexity (both qubit and fermionic) to implement GAG_{A} and GBG_{B} is 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}). Putting the above observations together, it follows that the circuit complexity of UtU_{t} is 𝒪⁡(n2+t3)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+t^{3}). As long as κ​t≤n\kappa t\leq n, this upper bound is tighter than the one which proof follows from the tt-doped definition, namely 𝒪⁡(n2​t)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}t).

The qubit (and not only fermionic) circuit complexity of 𝒪⁡(n2​t)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}t) for κ​t>n\kappa t>n can be found in a similar way as the complexity of 𝒪⁡(t3)\mathcal{O}(t^{3}) we showed for utu_{t} above. In particular, consider any κ\kappa-local non-Gaussian fermionic unitary Wt′W_{t^{\prime}} which participates in UtU_{t}. Using auxilliary Gaussian rotations, its generating Majorana operators can be mapped to {γ1,..,γκ}\{\gamma_{1},..,\gamma_{\kappa}\}, resulting in a unitary supported by the first ⌈κ2⌉\lceil\frac{\kappa}{2}\rceil qubits alone. The asymptotic qubit complexity of UtU_{t} is thus determined by that of remaining tt Gaussian layers, yielding 𝒪⁡(n2​t)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}t) as promised. ∎

This Proposition reveals that tt-doped fermion Gaussian unitaries allow not only a ‘spatial compression for the magic’, but also a compression of the circuit depth. Since our proof of Theorem 26 is constructive, this provides a useful method for compiling magic matchgate circuits, which might be used in practice to reduce the circuit depth.

III.4 tt-compressible Gaussian states

We now introduce the notion of tt-compressible fermionic Gaussian state, a class of states that includes the one of tt-doped Gaussian states. We now reiterate Definition 2 for convenience. Throughout this section, we assume that t∈[n]t\in[n].

Definition 31 (tt-compressible Gaussian state).

A state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is a tt-compressible (Gaussian) state if and only if it can be represented as |ψ⟩=G⁡(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)\ket{\psi}=G(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}), where GG is a Gaussian operation, and |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is a pure state supported solely on the first tt qubits.

A tt-doped Gaussian state is also a κ​t\kappa t-compressible Gaussian state because of Theorem 27. However, the reverse is not true because of circuit complexity arguments: tt-doped Gaussian states exhibit a circuit complexity of at most 𝒪⁡(n2​t)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}t). In contrast, a tt-compressible state features a circuit complexity of 𝒪⁡(n2+exp⁡(t))\mathcal{O}(n^{2}+\exp(t)), representing the complexity needed for implementing a single Gaussian operation and preparing a generic state supported on tt qubits.

In the subsequent Proposition, we elucidate the structure of the correlation matrix of any tt-compressible state, such as tt-doped states.

Proposition 32 (Correlation matrix of a tt-compressible Gaussian state).

The correlation matrix C⁡(|ψ⟩)C(\ket{\psi}) of a tt-compressible Gaussian state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} can be expressed as:

C⁡(|ψ⟩)=O​⨁j=1n(0λj−λj0)​OT,\displaystyle C(\ket{\psi})=O\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}0&\lambda_{j}\\ -\lambda_{j}&0\end{pmatrix}O^{T}, (S42)

where λj≤1\lambda_{j}\leq 1 for j∈[t]j\in[t] and λj=1\lambda_{j}=1 for j∈{t+1,…,n}j\in\{t+1,\dots,n\}, and O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n) is an orthogonal matrix.

Proof.

As per Definition 31, we represent |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} as |ψ⟩=G⁡(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)\ket{\psi}=G(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}), where GG is a Gaussian operation and |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is a pure state supported solely on the first tt qubits. Utilizing Lemma 16, we can express the correlation matrix C⁡(|ψ⟩)C(\ket{\psi}) as follows:

C⁡(|ψ⟩)\displaystyle C(\ket{\psi}) =Q​C​(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)​QT\displaystyle=QC(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}})Q^{T} (S43)
=Q⁡(C⁡(|ϕ⟩)⊕C⁡(|0n−t⟩))​QT,\displaystyle=Q\left(C(\ket{\phi})\oplus C(\ket{0^{n-t}})\right)Q^{T}, (S44)

where Q∈O⁡(2​n)Q\in\mathrm{O}(2n) is the orthogonal matrix associated to the Gaussian unitary GG. By Eq.(S7), we have:

C⁡(|0n−t⟩)=⨁j=1n−t(01−10).\displaystyle C(\ket{0^{n-t}})=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n-t}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}. (S45)

Since C⁡(|ϕ⟩)C(\ket{\phi}) is an antisymmetric real matrix, we can decompose it into its normal form (Lemma 16):

C⁡(|ϕ⟩)=Ot​⨁j=1t(0λj−λj0)​OtT\displaystyle C(\ket{\phi})=O_{t}\bigoplus_{j=1}^{t}\begin{pmatrix}0&\lambda_{j}\\ -\lambda_{j}&0\end{pmatrix}O_{t}^{T} (S46)

The proof concludes by definining O≔Q⁡(Ot⊕I2​n−2​t)O\coloneqq Q(O_{t}\oplus I_{2n-2t}). ∎

The previous proposition reveals that tt-compressible states exhibit at least n−tn-t normal eigenvalues which are exactly one. This motivates the following definition, in analogy to the stabilizer dimension and nullity defined in the stabilizer case [35, 63, 64], which found applications in resource theory of magic.

Definition 33 (Gaussian dimension and Gaussian nullity of a state).

The Gaussian dimension of a state is defined as the number of the normal eigenvalues of its correlation matrix which are equal to one, while the Gaussian nullity is defined as the number of the normal eigenvalues of its correlation matrix which are strictly less than one.

In the following, we show that this is also a sufficient condition for a state to be Gaussian tt-compressible.

Lemma 34 (Sufficient condition for tt-compressibility).

Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be an nn-qubit quantum state. If |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} has Gaussian dimension ≥n−t\geq n-t (or, equivalently, Gaussian nullity ≤t\leq t), then |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is a tt-compressible Gaussian state.

Proof.

The correlation matrix of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} can be written in its normal form as C⁡(|ψ⟩)=O​Λ​OTC(\ket{\psi})=O\Lambda O^{T}, where Λ≔⨁j=1n(0λj−λj0)\Lambda\coloneqq\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}0&\lambda_{j}\\ -\lambda_{j}&0\end{pmatrix}, and O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n). The {λj}i=1n\{\lambda_{j}\}^{n}_{i=1} are the normal eigenvalues such that the last n−tn-t are equal to one. Consider the state |ψ′⟩≔GO†​|ψ⟩\ket{\psi^{\prime}}\coloneqq G^{{\dagger}}_{O}\ket{\psi} where GOG_{O} is the Gaussian unitary associated with OO. Then, C⁡(ψ′)=OT​C​(|ψ⟩)​O=ΛC(\psi^{\prime})=O^{T}C(\ket{\psi})O=\Lambda. In particular,

Tr⁡(|ψ′⟩⟨ψ′|​Zk)=C​(ψ′)2​k−1,2​k=Λ2​k−1,2​k=1,\displaystyle\Tr(\ketbra{\psi^{\prime}}Z_k)=C(\psi^{\prime})_{2k-1,2k}=\Lambda_{2k-1,2k}=1, (S47)

for each k∈{t+1,…,n}k\in\{t+1,\dots,n\}. Therefore, |ψ′⟩\ket{\psi^{\prime}} must be of the form |ψ′⟩=|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩\ket{\psi^{\prime}}=\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}, where |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is an arbitrary state on the first tt qubits. Therefore, we have |ψ⟩=GO​(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)\ket{\psi}=G_{O}(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}), which is a tt-compressible state. ∎

Hence, Proposition 32 and Lemma 34 prove the following.

Proposition 35 (Equivalence between tt-compressibily and n−tn-t Gaussian dimension).

A nn-qubit state is tt-compressible if and only if its Gaussian dimension is at least n−tn-t (or, equivalently, its Gaussian nullity is at most tt).

Note that Proposition 35 also proves that a quantum state is a pure Gaussian state if and only if its Gaussian dimension is nn. Furthermore, as a direct consequence of the proof of Lemma 34, we establish that the Gaussian unitary associated with a tt-compressible Gaussian state can be selected as the Gaussian unitary corresponding to any orthogonal matrix placing its correlation matrix in the normal form (Lemma 16). This is summarized as follows:

Lemma 36.

Every tt-compressible Gaussian state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} can be written as |ψ⟩≔GO​(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)\ket{\psi}\coloneqq G_{O}(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}), where GOG_{O} is chosen as the Gaussian unitary associated with an orthogonal matrix O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n) that arranges its correlation matrix in the normal form described in Lemma 16, and |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is a state supported on tt qubits.

Supplementary Material IV: Tomography algorithm

In this section, we present a detailed and rigorous analysis of the tomography algorithm for tt-compressible states outlined in the main text (Algorithm 1). Throughout this section, we assume that t∈[n]t\in[n].

IV.1 Useful lemmas and subroutines

Let us start with a Lemma, which gives a sample complexity upper bound to estimate the correlation matrix of a state using single-qubit Pauli-basis measurements. We recall that the correlation matrix of a state ρ\rho is a real antisymmetric matrix, defined as:

[C⁡(ρ)]j,k=Tr⁡(O(j,k)​ρ),\displaystyle[C(\rho)]_{j,k}=\mathrm{Tr}(O^{(j,k)}\rho), (S48)

where O(j,k)≔−i​γj​γkO^{(j,k)}\coloneqq-i\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k}, for j<k∈[2​n]j<k\in[2n] (and the other elements are given by the antisymmetricity of the matrix). Note that O(j,k)O^{(j,k)} are Pauli observables. Thus, we have a total of M≔n⁡(2​n−1)M\coloneqq n(2n-1) Pauli expectation values to estimate.

Lemma 37 (Sample complexity for estimating the correlation matrix by Pauli measurements).

Let εc,δ>0\varepsilon_{c},\delta>0. Assume to have access to N≥Nc​(n,εc,δ)N\geq N_{c}(n,\varepsilon_{c},\delta), with

Nc​(n,εc,δ)≔⌈8​n3​(2​n−1)εc2​log⁡(2​n​(2​n−1)δ)⌉,\displaystyle N_{c}(n,\varepsilon_{c},\delta)\coloneqq\left\lceil\frac{8n^{3}(2n-1)}{\varepsilon_{c}^{2}}\log\!\left(\frac{2n(2n-1)}{\delta}\right)\right\rceil, (S49)

copies of an nn-qubit state ρ\rho. Utilizing only NN single-copies measurements in the Pauli basis, with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta, we can construct an anti-symmetric real matrix C^\hat{C} such that it satisfies:

‖C^−C⁡(ρ)‖∞≤εc.\displaystyle\norm{\hat{C}-C(\rho)}_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon_{c}. (S50)
Proof.

Let ε>0\varepsilon>0 an accuracy parameter to be fixed. For each j<k∈[2​n]j<k\in[2n], we measure N′N^{\prime} copies of ρ\rho in the Pauli basis corresponding to O(j,k)O^{(j,k)}, obtaining outcomes {Xm(j,k)}m=1N′\{X^{(j,k)}_{m}\}^{N^{\prime}}_{m=1}, where Xm(j,k)∈{−1,+1}X^{(j,k)}_{m}\in\{-1,+1\}. Let C^j,k≔1N′​∑m=1N′Xm(j,k)\hat{C}_{j,k}\coloneqq\frac{1}{N^{\prime}}\sum^{N^{\prime}}_{m=1}X^{(j,k)}_{m}. Hoeffding’s inequality (specifically Corollary 9) implies that N′≥(4/(2​ε2))​log⁡(2​M/δ)N^{\prime}\geq(4/(2\varepsilon^{2}))\log(2M/\delta) suffices to guarantee that, with probability at least 1−δ/M1-\delta/M, we have |C^j,k−Tr⁡(O(j,k)​ρ)|<ε\lvert\hat{C}_{j,k}-\mathrm{Tr}(O^{(j,k)}\rho)\rvert<\varepsilon. By using the union bound, we conclude that the probability that this holds for any j<k∈[2​n]j<k\in[2n] is at least 1−δ1-\delta. More specifically:

Pr(∀j<k∈[2n]:|C^j,k−Tr(O(j,k)ρ)|<ε)\displaystyle\operatorname{Pr}\!\left(\forall\,j<k\in[2n]:\lvert\hat{C}_{j,k}-\mathrm{Tr}(O^{(j,k)}\rho)\rvert<\varepsilon\right) =1−Pr(∃j<k∈[2n]:|C^j,k−Tr(O(j,k)ρ)|≥ε)\displaystyle=1-\operatorname{Pr}\!\left(\exists\,j<k\in[2n]:\lvert\hat{C}_{j,k}-\mathrm{Tr}(O^{(j,k)}\rho)\rvert\geq\varepsilon\right) (S51)
≥1−∑j<k∈[2​n]Pr⁡(|C^j,k−Tr⁡(O(j,k)​ρ)|≥ε)\displaystyle\geq 1-\sum_{j<k\in[2n]}\operatorname{Pr}\!\left(\lvert\hat{C}_{j,k}-\mathrm{Tr}(O^{(j,k)}\rho)\rvert\geq\varepsilon\right) (S52)
≥1−δ.\displaystyle\geq 1-\delta. (S53)

Therefore, the total number of measurements needed is N=N′​MN=N^{\prime}M. Now, we can conclude by transferring the error to the operator norm. Let A≔C^−C⁡(ρ)A\coloneqq\hat{C}-C(\rho). For the definition of the operator norm, we have ‖A‖∞≔sup|ψ⟩|⟨ψ|​A†​A​|ψ⟩|\norm{A}_{\infty}\coloneqq\sup_{\ket{\psi}}\sqrt{\left|\bra{\psi}A^{{\dagger}}A\ket{\psi}\right|}. Thus, we have:

|⟨ψ|​A†​A​|ψ⟩|\displaystyle\left|\bra{\psi}A^{{\dagger}}A\ket{\psi}\right| ≤∑i,j,k=12​n|⟨ψ|​|i⟩⟨i|​A†​|j⟩⟨j|​A​|k⟩⟨k|​|ψ⟩|=2​n​ε2​∑i,k=12​n|⟨ψ|i⟩|​|⟨k|ψ⟩|≤4​n2​ε2\displaystyle\leq\sum^{2n}_{i,j,k=1}\left|\bra{\psi}\outerproduct{i}{i}A^{{\dagger}}\outerproduct{j}{j}A\outerproduct{k}{k}\ket{\psi}\right|=2n\varepsilon^{2}\sum^{2n}_{i,k=1}\left|\innerproduct{\psi}{i}\right|\left|\innerproduct{k}{\psi}\right|\leq 4n^{2}\varepsilon^{2} (S54)

where, in the first step, we inserted the resolution of the identity and applied the triangle inequality, in the second step, we applied the upper bound on each matrix element, and, in the last step, we used the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality. Hence, we have ‖C^−C⁡(ρ)‖∞≤2​n​ε\norm{\hat{C}-C(\rho)}_{\infty}\leq 2n\varepsilon. We conclude by choosing εc≔ε/2​n\varepsilon_{c}\coloneqq\varepsilon/2n. ∎

While the sequential estimation of individual correlation matrix entries by measurements in the Pauli basis, as described above, may not be the most sample-efficient approach, it might be convenient to adopt in an experiment because of its easy implementation scheme. However, instead of independently estimating each correlation matrix entry, one could choose to simultaneously measure mutually commuting observables [66] or utilize the fermionic classical shadow protocol introduced in [67, 58, 68]. This refinement would lead to a reduction in sample complexity by a factor of nn, at the cost of implementing a slightly more complicated measurement scheme.

For completeness, we present now a Lemma which gives a sample complexity upper bound for estimating the correlation matrix using a commuting observables measurement scheme. The idea is to partition the observables O(j,k)≔−i​γj​γkO^{(j,k)}\coloneqq-i\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k}, for j<k∈[2​n]j<k\in[2n] into disjoint sets of commuting observables. Subsequently, one employs the fact that commuting Pauli observables can be measured simultaneously via a Clifford measurement [66, 83]. A crucial observation is that two different Pauli observables of the form −i​γj​γk-i\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k} commute if and only if they are associated with different Majorana operators. Using this observation, we can partition these M=(2​n−1)​nM=(2n-1)n observables into 2​n−12n-1 disjoint sets, each containing nn commuting Pauli observables. We refer to [66] Appendix C for details of such a partition, and we omit repeating the construction here. However, we point out that the required Clifford transformations can be chosen to be Gaussian as well.

Lemma 38 (Sample complexity for estimating the correlation matrix by grouping commuting observables).

Let εc,δ>0\varepsilon_{c},\delta>0. Assume to have access to N≥Nc​(n,εc,δ)N\geq N_{c}(n,\varepsilon_{c},\delta), with

Nc​(n,εc,δ)≔⌈8​n2​(2​n−1)εc2​log⁡(2​n​(2​n−1)δ)⌉,\displaystyle N_{c}(n,\varepsilon_{c},\delta)\coloneqq\left\lceil\frac{8n^{2}(2n-1)}{\varepsilon_{c}^{2}}\log\!\left(\frac{2n(2n-1)}{\delta}\right)\right\rceil, (S55)

copies of an nn-qubit state ρ\rho. Utilizing NN single-copy (Gaussian) measurements, with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta, we can construct an anti-symmetric real matrix C^\hat{C} such that it satisfies:

‖C^−C⁡(ρ)‖∞≤εc.\displaystyle\norm{\hat{C}-C(\rho)}_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon_{c}. (S56)
Proof.

For each of the 2​n−12n-1 sets of commuting Pauli, we find the Clifford UU that allows us to simultaneously measure such commuting Pauli in the given set, i.e. we map each of the nn Pauli to {Zk}k=1n\{Z_{k}\}^{n}_{k=1}. Now this Clifford can also be chosen to be Gaussian. Indeed, the key constraint on UU is that each of the different Paulis of the form −i​γj​γk-i\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k} with j<k∈[2​n]j<k\in[2n] (where pairs (j,k)(j,k) are non-overlapping since these Paulis commute) is mapped to {Zk}k=1n\{Z_{k}\}^{n}_{k=1} with Zk:=−i​γ2​k−1​γ2​kZ_{k}:=-i\gamma_{2k-1}\gamma_{2k}. This constraint can be satisfied by using a Gaussian operation associated to the orthogonal matrix which is a permutation of the Majorana indices from the commuting Paulis into the Majorana indices from the ZZ-Paulis. Consequently, we measure N′N^{\prime} copies of U​ρ​U†U\rho U^{\dagger} in the computational basis. Thus, for each O(j,k)O^{(j,k)}, we obtain outcomes {Xm(j,k)}m=1N′\{X^{(j,k)}_{m}\}^{N^{\prime}}_{m=1}, where Xm(j,k)∈{−1,+1}X^{(j,k)}_{m}\in\{-1,+1\}. The unbiased estimators are C^j,k≔1N′​∑m=1N′Xm(j,k)\hat{C}_{j,k}\coloneqq\frac{1}{N^{\prime}}\sum^{N^{\prime}}_{m=1}X^{(j,k)}_{m}. As before, Hoeffding’s inequality and union bound imply that N′≥(2/ε2)​log⁡(2​M/δ)N^{\prime}\geq(2/\varepsilon^{2})\log(2M/\delta) suffices to guarantee that the probability of |C^j,k−Tr⁡(O(j,k)​ρ)|<ε\lvert\hat{C}_{j,k}-\mathrm{Tr}(O^{(j,k)}\rho)\rvert<\varepsilon holding for each j<k∈[2​n]j<k\in[2n] is at least 1−δ1-\delta. Therefore, the total number of measurements needed is N=N′​(2​n−1)N=N^{\prime}(2n-1). We can conclude as in the previous Lemma. ∎

Lemma 39 (Perturbation bounds on the normal eigenvalues of correlation matrices).

Let AA and BB be two 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n anti-symmetric real matrices with normal eigenvalues {λk​(A)}k=1n\{\lambda_{k}(A)\}^{n}_{k=1} and {λk​(B)}k=1n\{\lambda_{k}(B)\}^{n}_{k=1} respectively ordered in increasing order. Then, we have:

|λk​(A)−λk​(B)|≤‖A−B‖∞,\displaystyle|\lambda_{k}(A)-\lambda_{k}(B)|\leq\norm{A-B}_{\infty}, (S57)

for any k∈[n]k\in[n].

Proof.

This follows from the fact that C≔i​AC\coloneqq iA and D≔i​BD\coloneqq iB are Hermitian matrices. Applying Weyl’s Perturbation Theorem (see Ref. [84], section VI), which states that two 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n Hermitian matrices CC and DD, with eigenvalues c1≤⋯≤c2​nc_{1}\leq\dots\leq c_{2n} and d1≤⋯≤d2​nd_{1}\leq\dots\leq d_{2n}, satisfy:

‖C−D‖∞≥maxj∈[n]⁡|cj−dj|.\displaystyle\norm{C-D}_{\infty}\geq\max_{j\in[n]}|c_{j}-d_{j}|. (S58)

Since AA and BB are antisymmetric, their eigenvalues are {±i​λk​(A)}k=1n\{\pm i\lambda_{k}(A)\}^{n}_{k=1} and {±i​λk​(B)}k=1n\{\pm i\lambda_{k}(B)\}^{n}_{k=1} respectively. Hence, the eigenvalues of CC and DD are {±λk​(A)}k=1n\{\pm\lambda_{k}(A)\}^{n}_{k=1} and {±λk​(B)}k=1n\{\pm\lambda_{k}(B)\}^{n}_{k=1} respectively. This implies that:

‖A−B‖∞=‖C−D‖∞≥maxj∈[2​n]⁡|cj−dj|=maxk∈[n]⁡|λk​(A)−λk​(B)|.\displaystyle\norm{A-B}_{\infty}=\norm{C-D}_{\infty}\geq\max_{j\in[2n]}|c_{j}-d_{j}|=\max_{k\in[n]}|\lambda_{k}(A)-\lambda_{k}(B)|. (S59)

∎

To formalize our learning algorithm, it is useful to invoke the following well-known lemma.

Lemma 40 (Quantum Union Bound [70, 85, 86]).

Let ε1,…,εM>0\varepsilon_{1},\dots,\varepsilon_{M}>0, where M∈ℕM\in\mathbb{N}. Let {Pi}i=1M\{P_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} be projectors, and ρ\rho be a quantum state. If Tr⁡(Pi​ρ)≥1−εi\operatorname{Tr}(P_{i}\rho)\geq 1-\varepsilon_{i} for all i∈[M]i\in[M], then

‖ρ−PM​…​P1​ρ​P1​…​PMTr⁡(PM​…​P1​ρ​P1​…​PM)‖1≤2​∑i∈[M]εi.\displaystyle\left\|\rho-\frac{P_{M}\dots P_{1}\rho P_{1}\dots P_{M}}{\operatorname{Tr}(P_{M}\dots P_{1}\rho P_{1}\dots P_{M})}\right\|_{1}\leq 2\sqrt{\sum_{i\in[M]}\varepsilon_{i}}\,. (S60)

We now leverage this known lemma to prove the following.

Lemma 41.

Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be a tt-compressible Gaussian state. Given an estimate C^\hat{C} for the correlation matrix C⁡(|ψ⟩)C(\ket{\psi}), there exists a Gaussian operation G^\hat{G} such that:

dtr​(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩,G^†​|ψ⟩)≤(n−t)​‖C^−C⁡(|ψ⟩)‖∞,\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\phi}\!\otimes\!\ket{0^{n-t}}\!,\hat{G}^{{\dagger}}\!\ket{\psi})\leq\sqrt{(n-t)\norm{\hat{C}-C(\ket{\psi})}_{\infty}\!}, (S61)

where |ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}} corresponds to the post-measurement state obtained by measuring the last n−tn-t qubits of the state G^†​|ψ⟩\hat{G}^{{\dagger}}\ket{\psi} in the computational basis and obtaining the outcome corresponding to |0n−t⟩\ket{0^{n-t}}. This event occurs with a probability of at least 1−(n−t)​‖C^−C‖∞1-(n-t)\norm{\hat{C}-C}_{\infty}.

Proof.

According to Proposition 32, the correlation matrix C≔C⁡(|ψ⟩)C\coloneqq C(\ket{\psi}) can be put in the form C=O​Λ​OTC=O\Lambda O^{\rm T}, where O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n) and Λ=i​⨁j=1nλj​(C)​Y\Lambda=i\bigoplus^{n}_{j=1}\lambda_{j}(C)Y. Here, λj≤1\lambda_{j}\leq 1 for j∈[t]j\in[t] and λj=1\lambda_{j}=1 for j∈{t+1,…​n}j\in\{t+1,\dots n\}, and YY represents the YY-Pauli matrix. Let εc≔‖C^−C‖∞\varepsilon_{c}\coloneqq\norm{\hat{C}-C}_{\infty}, then we have (because of Lemma 39) that |λj​(C^)−λj​(C)|≤εc|\lambda_{j}(\hat{C})-\lambda_{j}(C)|\leq\varepsilon_{c}, where {λj​(C^)}j=1n\{\lambda_{j}(\hat{C})\}^{n}_{j=1} and {λj​(C)}j=1n\{\lambda_{j}(C)\}^{n}_{j=1} are the normal eigenvalues of the matrices C^\hat{C} and CC respectively. Thus, we have:

λm​(C^)≥1−εc,\displaystyle\lambda_{m}(\hat{C})\geq 1-\varepsilon_{c}, (S62)

for m∈{t+1,…​n}m\in\{t+1,\dots n\}. We can now express the real anti-symmetric matrix C^\hat{C} in its normal form C^=O^​Λ^​O^T\hat{C}=\hat{O}\hat{\Lambda}\hat{O}^{T}, where O^∈O⁡(2​n)\hat{O}\in\mathrm{O}(2n) is an orthogonal matrix and Λ^\hat{\Lambda} is a matrix of the form Λ^=i​⨁j=1nλj​(C^)​Y\hat{\Lambda}=i\bigoplus^{n}_{j=1}\lambda_{j}(\hat{C})Y, with λj​(C^)∈ℝ\lambda_{j}(\hat{C})\in\mathbb{R} for any j∈[n]j\in[n]. Next, consider the state |ψ′⟩≔G^†​|ψ⟩|\psi^{\prime}\rangle\coloneqq\hat{G}^{{\dagger}}\ket{\psi}, where G^\hat{G} is the Gaussian unitary associated to O^T\hat{O}^{T}. It holds that |C​(ψ′)j,k−(Λ^)j,k|≤εc\lvert C(\psi^{\prime})_{j,k}-(\hat{\Lambda})_{j,k}\rvert\leq\varepsilon_{c}, where we used that C⁡(ψ′)=O^T​C​(|ψ⟩)​O^C(\psi^{\prime})=\hat{O}^{T}C(\ket{\psi})\hat{O}, Λ^=O^T​C^​O^\hat{\Lambda}=\hat{O}^{T}\hat{C}\hat{O}, Cauchy-Schwarz and the definition of infinity norm. Therefore, we have C​(ψ′)j,k≥(Λ^)j,k−εcC(\psi^{\prime})_{j,k}\geq(\hat{\Lambda})_{j,k}-\varepsilon_{c}. In particular, for m∈{t+1,…,n}m\in\{t+1,\dots,n\}, we get:

Tr⁡(Zm​ψ′)\displaystyle\Tr(Z_m \psi^{\prime}) =C​(ψ′)2​m−1,2​m\displaystyle=C(\psi^{\prime})_{2m-1,2m} (S63)
≥(Λ^)2​m−1,2​m−εc\displaystyle\geq(\hat{\Lambda})_{2m-1,2m}-\varepsilon_{c} (S64)
=λm​(C^)−εc\displaystyle=\lambda_{m}(\hat{C})-\varepsilon_{c} (S65)
≥1−2​εc,\displaystyle\geq 1-2\varepsilon_{c}, (S66)

where Zm=−i​γ2​m−1​γ2​mZ_{m}=-i\gamma_{2m-1}\gamma_{2m} is the ZZ-Pauli operator acting on the mm-th qubit and in the last step we used Eq.(S62). Therefore, we also have Tr⁡(|0⟩⟨0|m​ψ′)≥1−εc\Tr(\ketbra{0}{0}_m \psi^{\prime})\geq 1-\varepsilon_{c}. By using the Quantum Union Bound (Lemma 40), we have:

dtr​(|ψ′⟩,|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)≤(n−t)​εc,\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi^{\prime}},\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}})\leq\sqrt{(n-t)\varepsilon_{c}}, (S67)

where |ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}} is the post-measurement state after having measured the outcomes corresponding to |0n−t⟩\ket{0^{n-t}} in the last n−tn-t qubits. By Lemma 40, this scenario occurs with probability at least 1−(n−t)​εc1-(n-t)\varepsilon_{c}. ∎

In the following, we mention the guarantees of a full pure state tomography algorithm, which demonstrates optimal dependence on the number of qubits and uses only single-copies measurements, albeit with a trade-off in accuracy compared to other algorithms [3, 87]. This is an example of a procedure that we can utilize in our tt-qubits full state tomography step of our learning algorithm.

Lemma 42 (Fast state tomography [65]).

For any unknown nn-qubit pure state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle, there exists a quantum algorithm that, utilizing Ntom​(n,ε,δ)≔𝒪⁡(2n​n​log⁡(1/δ)​ε−4)N_{\mathrm{tom}}(n,\varepsilon,\delta)\coloneqq\mathcal{O}\!\left(2^{n}n\log(1 / \delta)\varepsilon^{-4}\right) copies of |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle and Ttom​(n,ε,δ)≔𝒪⁡(4n​n3​log⁡(1/δ)​ε−5)T_{\mathrm{tom}}(n,\varepsilon,\delta)\coloneqq\mathcal{O}\!\left(4^{n}n^{3}\log(1 / \delta)\varepsilon^{-5}\right) time, generates a classical representation of a state |ψ~⟩|\tilde{\psi}\rangle that is ε\varepsilon-close to |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle in trace distance with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. Furthermore, the algorithm requires only single-copy Clifford measurements and classical post-processing.

Next, we provide a lemma that is useful in the proof of the subsequent Theorem 44.

Lemma 43 (Boosting the probability of success).

Let δ>0\delta>0 and N′∈ℕN^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}. Consider an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that succeeds with a probability of psucc≥34p_{\mathrm{succ}}\geq\frac{3}{4}. If we execute 𝒜\mathcal{A} a total of m≥⌈2​N′+24​log⁡(1δ)⌉m\geq\lceil 2N^{\prime}+24\log\!\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)\rceil times, then 𝒜\mathcal{A} will succeed at least N′N^{\prime} times with a probability of at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Proof.

We will employ a Chernoff bound 7 to establish this result. Define binary random variables {Xi}i=1m\{X_{i}\}^{m}_{i=1} as follows:

Xi={1if 𝒜 succeeds,0if 𝒜 fails.\displaystyle X_{i}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $\mathcal{A}$ succeeds},\\ 0&\text{if $\mathcal{A}$ fails}.\end{cases} (S68)

Define X^≔∑i=1mXi\hat{X}\coloneqq\sum^{m}_{i=1}X_{i}. We have 𝔼⁡[X^]=m​psucc\mathbb{E}[\hat{X}]=mp_{\mathrm{succ}}. Moreover, we aim to upper bound by δ\delta the probability that 𝒜\mathcal{A} succeeds fewer than N′N^{\prime} times, which is Pr⁡(X^≤N′)\operatorname{Pr}\!\left(\hat{X}\leq N^{\prime}\right). We first write it as Pr⁡(X^≤N′)=Pr⁡(X^≤(1−α)​𝔼​[X^])\operatorname{Pr}\!\left(\hat{X}\leq N^{\prime}\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\!\left(\hat{X}\leq\left(1-\alpha\right)\mathbb{E}[\hat{X}]\right), where we defined α≔1−N′m​psucc\alpha\coloneqq 1-\frac{N^{\prime}}{mp_{\mathrm{succ}}}. Note that α\alpha satisfies α≥13\alpha\geq\frac{1}{3}, if

m≥2​N′,\displaystyle m\geq 2N^{\prime}, (S69)

exploiting the fact that psucc≥34p_{\mathrm{succ}}\geq\frac{3}{4}. Applying the Chernoff bound, we obtain:

Pr⁡(X^≤(1−α)​𝔼​[X^])≤exp⁡(−α2​𝔼​[X^]2)=exp⁡(−α22​psucc​m).\displaystyle\operatorname{Pr}\!\left(\hat{X}\leq(1-\alpha)\mathbb{E}[\hat{X}]\right)\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{\alpha^{2}\mathbb{E}[\hat{X}]}{2}\right)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}p_{\mathrm{succ}}m\right). (S70)

This is upper bounded by δ\delta if

m≥2psucc​α2​log⁡(1δ).\displaystyle m\geq\frac{2}{p_{\mathrm{succ}}\alpha^{2}}\log\!\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right). (S71)

Therefore, choosing mm as follows satisfies Eq. (S69) and Eq. (S71):

m≥2​N′+2(34)​(13)2​log⁡(1δ)=2​N′+24​log⁡(1δ),\displaystyle m\geq 2N^{\prime}+\frac{2}{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}}\log\!\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)=2N^{\prime}+24\log\!\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right), (S72)

where we used the fact that psucc≥34p_{\mathrm{succ}}\geq\frac{3}{4} and α≥13\alpha\geq\frac{1}{3}. ∎

IV.2 Joining the pieces: proof of correctness

We now present the main theorem which puts together the lemmas we have discussed. It demonstrates that to learn tt-doped fermionic Gaussian states, or more generally tt-compressible Gaussian states, with t=𝒪⁡(log⁡(n))t=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\log(n)\right), only resources scaling polynomially in the number of qubits are required.

Theorem 44 (Efficient learning of tt-compressible Gaussian states).

Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be a tt-compressible Gaussian state, and consider ε,δ∈(0,1]\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1]. By utilizing

N\displaystyle N ≥256​n5ε4​log⁡(12​n2δ)+2​Ntom​(t,ε2,δ3)+24​log⁡(3δ)\displaystyle\geq\frac{256n^{5}}{\varepsilon^{4}}\log\!\left(\frac{12n^{2}}{\delta}\right)+2N_{\mathrm{tom}}\!\left(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{3}\right)+24\log\!\left(\frac{3}{\delta}\right) (S73)

single-copy measurements and

T\displaystyle T ≥𝒪⁡(n3)+Ttom​(t,ε2,δ3)\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{O}(n^{3})+T_{\mathrm{tom}}\!\left(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{3}\right) (S74)

computational time, Algorithm 1 yields a classical representation of a state |ψ^⟩|\hat{\psi}\rangle, satisfying dtr​(|ψ^⟩,|ψ⟩)≤εd_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\psi}\rangle,\ket{\psi})\leq\varepsilon with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta.

Here, Ntom​(t,ε2,δ3)N_{\mathrm{tom}}(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{3}) and Ttom​(t,ε2,δ3)T_{\mathrm{tom}}(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{3}) respectively denote the number of copies and computational time sufficient for full state tomography of a tt-qubit state with an ε/2\varepsilon/2 accuracy and a failure probability of at most δ/3\delta/3 (using the notation of Lemma 42).

Proof.

The learning procedure is outlined in Algorithm 1 in the main text. We now establish its efficiency and correctness. According to Lemma 38, Nc​(n,εc,δ/3)N_{c}(n,\varepsilon_{c},\delta/3) single copies of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} are sufficient to construct an anti-symmetric real matrix C^\hat{C} such that ‖C^−C‖∞≤εc\norm{\hat{C}-C}_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon_{c} with a probability of at least 1−δ/31-\delta/3, where CC is the correlation matrix of ρ\rho. Here, we set εc≔ε2/(4​(n−t))\varepsilon_{c}\coloneqq\varepsilon^{2}/(4(n-t)). Then, we can find the orthogonal matrix O^∈O⁡(2​n)\hat{O}\in\mathrm{O}(2n) such that it puts C^\hat{C} in its normal form Eq.(1), which can be performed in 𝒪⁡(n3)\mathcal{O}\!\left(n^{3}\right) time. Employing this, we construct the associated Gaussian unitary G^\hat{G} (a task achievable in time 𝒪⁡(n3)\mathcal{O}\!\left(n^{3}\right), see [38, 58]). Subsequently, we consider the state G^†​|ψ⟩\hat{G}^{{\dagger}}\ket{\psi}. As per Lemma 41, we have

dtr​(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩,G^†​|ψ⟩)≤ε2,\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}},\hat{G}^{{\dagger}}\ket{\psi})\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}, (S75)

where |ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}} corresponds to the post-measurement state obtained by measuring the last n−tn-t qubits of the state G^†​|ψ⟩\hat{G}^{{\dagger}}\ket{\psi} in the computational basis and obtaining the outcome corresponding to |0n−t⟩\ket{0^{n-t}}. The probability of such an occurrence, as per Lemma 41, is at least 1−ε2/4≥3/41-\varepsilon^{2}/4\geq 3/4. Thus, the algorithm proceeds iteratively by querying a total of mm copies of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}. In each iteration, it applies the unitary G^†\hat{G}^{{\dagger}} to |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} and computational basis measurements on the last n−tn-t qubits. By choosing m≔⌈2​Ntom​(t,ε/2,δ/3)+24​log⁡(3/δ)⌉m\coloneqq\lceil 2N_{\mathrm{tom}}(t,\varepsilon/2,\delta/3)+24\log(3/\delta)\rceil, it is guaranteed that the measurements outcome corresponding to |0n−t⟩\ket{0^{n-t}} occurred at least Ntom​(t,ε/2,δ/3)N_{\mathrm{tom}}(t,\varepsilon/2,\delta/3) with probability at least 1−δ/31-\delta/3 (this follows by Lemma 43). Applying the tomography algorithm of Lemma 42 to the first tt qubits of all the copies where we obtained the outcome corresponding to |0n−t⟩\ket{0^{n-t}}, we obtain an output state |ϕ^⟩|\hat{\phi}\rangle such that it is guaranteed that:

dtr​(|ϕ^⟩,|ϕ⟩)≤ε2,\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\phi}\rangle,\ket{\phi})\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}, (S76)

with a probability of at least 1−δ/31-\delta/3. Our output state is |ψ^⟩≔G^​(|ϕ^⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)|\hat{\psi}\rangle\coloneqq\hat{G}(|\hat{\phi}\rangle\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}), and the information about such a state is provided in the output by providing the orthogonal matrix O^∈O⁡(2​n)\hat{O}\in\mathrm{O}(2n), which identifies G^\hat{G}, and the tt-qubit state |ϕ^⟩|\hat{\phi}\rangle.

Considering the trace distance between |ψ^⟩|\hat{\psi}\rangle and |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} and applying the triangle inequality with G^​(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)\hat{G}(|\phi\rangle\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}) as the reference state, we have:

dtr​(|ψ^⟩,|ψ⟩)≤dtr​(|ϕ^⟩,|ϕ⟩)+dtr​(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩,G^†​|ψ⟩),\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\psi}\rangle,\ket{\psi})\leq d_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\phi}\rangle,\ket{\phi})+d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}},\hat{G}^{{\dagger}}\ket{\psi}), (S77)

where in the last step we use the unitary-invariance of the trace distance and dtr​(|ϕ^⟩⊗|0n−t⟩,|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)=dtr​(|ϕ^⟩,|ϕ⟩)d_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\phi}\rangle\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}},|\phi\rangle\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}})=d_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\phi}\rangle,\ket{\phi}). The algorithm’s overall failure probability is contingent on the potential failure of any of the three subroutines—specifically, correlation matrix estimation, measurement of the last n−tn-t qubits, and the tomography protocol. Each subroutine is associated with a failure probability of at most δ/3\delta/3. Consequently, by the union bound, the algorithm’s total failure probability is at most δ\delta. Utilizing Eqs.(S75),(S76),(S77) and assuming the case in which the algorithm does not fail, we deduce dtr​(|ψ^⟩,|ψ⟩)≤εd_{\mathrm{tr}}(|\hat{\psi}\rangle,\ket{\psi})\leq\varepsilon. The overall sample complexity is determined by the number of copies needed to estimate the correlation matrix Nc​(n,εc,δ/3)N_{c}(n,\varepsilon_{c},\delta/3) plus the copies mm for tomography, i.e., a total number of copies

N=⌈256​n5ε4​log⁡(12​n2δ)+2​Ntom​(t,ε2,δ3)+24​log⁡(3δ)⌉,\displaystyle N=\left\lceil\frac{256n^{5}}{\varepsilon^{4}}\log\!\left(\frac{12n^{2}}{\delta}\right)+2N_{\mathrm{tom}}\!\left(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{3}\right)+24\log\!\left(\frac{3}{\delta}\right)\right\rceil, (S78)

suffices, which is 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n)+exp⁡(t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(n)+\exp(t)). On the other hand, the time complexity involves post-processing of the estimated correlation matrix, requiring 𝒪⁡(n3)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}) time, and the time-complexity for full-state tomography which is 𝒪⁡(exp⁡(t))\mathcal{O}(\exp(t)). ∎

Remark 45.

The output state of Algorithm 1 is |ψ^⟩≔G^​(|ϕ^⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)|\hat{\psi}\rangle\coloneqq\hat{G}(|\hat{\phi}\rangle\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}). Specifically, to provide a classical representation of |ψ^⟩|\hat{\psi}\rangle in the output, it suffices to give the orthogonal matrix O^∈O⁡(2​n)\hat{O}\in\mathrm{O}(2n) associated with G^\hat{G} and the classical description of the tt-qubit state |ϕ^⟩|\hat{\phi}\rangle. Therefore, the memory necessary to store the classical description of the state outputted by Algorithm 1 is 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n,2t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(n,2^{t})), similarly to its time and sample complexity.

Supplementary Material V: Testing tt-compressible states

In this section, we address property testing problem, i.e. the problem of determining whether a state is close or far from the set of states tt-compressible states (or equivalently we test the Gaussian dimension of a state). We begin by establishing an upper bound on the trace distance between a state and the set of tt-compressible Gaussian states. Subsequently, we present a lower bound on the same quantity. Finally, we leverage these two bounds to develop a testing algorithm for tt-compressible Gaussian states.

We note that the testing problem in the context of fermionic Gaussian states (t=0t=0) was also unsolved. However, a forthcoming paper [76] addresses the testing problem for general, possibly mixed, fermionic Gaussian states. Here, we generalize the results presented in [76] regarding Gaussian testing to the scenario of tt-compressible Gaussian states.

V.1 Upper bound on the trace distance from the set of tt-compressible states

We observed in Lemma 34 that when n−tn-t normal eigenvalues of a state’s correlation matrix are precisely one, the state is a tt-compressible state. However, when these eigenvalues are close to one, we may inquire about the existence of a tt-compressible state in close proximity. This inquiry is formalized in the subsequent Proposition 46.

Proposition 46 (Check the closeness to a tt-compressible Gaussian state).

Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be a quantum state. Let {λi}i=1n\{\lambda_{i}\}^{n}_{i=1} be the normal eigenvalues of its correlation matrix ordered in increasing order. Then, there exists a tt-compressible Gaussian state |ψt⟩\ket{\psi_t} such that:

dtr​(|ψt⟩,|ψ⟩)≤∑k=t+1n12​(1−λk).\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi_t },\ket{\psi})\leq\sqrt{\sum^{n}_{k=t+1}\frac{1}{2}(1-\lambda_{k})}. (S79)

In particular, |ψt⟩\ket{\psi_t } can be chosen as |ψt⟩≔GO​(|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)\ket{\psi_t }\coloneqq G_{O}(\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}}), where GOG_{O} is the Gaussian unitary associated with the orthogonal matrix O∈O⁡(2​n)O\in\mathrm{O}(2n) that puts the correlation matrix of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} in its normal form (Lemma 16), and |ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}} is the state obtained by projecting the state GO†​|ψ⟩G^{{\dagger}}_{O}\ket{\psi} onto the zero state on the last n−tn-t qubits.

Proof.

We can define the state |ψ′⟩≔GO†​|ψ⟩\ket{\psi^{\prime}}\coloneqq G^{{\dagger}}_{O}\ket{\psi}. We have:

Tr⁡(|ψ′⟩⟨ψ′|​Zk)=C​(ψ′)2​k−1,2​k=Λ2​k−1,2​k=λk=1−(1−λk),\displaystyle\Tr(\ketbra{\psi^{\prime}}Z_k)=C(\psi^{\prime})_{2k-1,2k}=\Lambda_{2k-1,2k}=\lambda_{k}=1-(1-\lambda_{k}), (S80)

for each k∈{t+1,…,n}k\in\{t+1,\dots,n\}. By using that Zk=2​|0⟩⟨0|k−IZ_{k}=2\outerproduct{0}{0}_{k}-I, we have:

Tr⁡(|ψ′⟩⟨ψ′|​|0⟩⟨0|k)=1−(1−λk)2\displaystyle\Tr(\ketbra{\psi^{\prime}}\ketbra{0}_k)=1-\frac{(1-\lambda_{k})}{2} (S81)

By Quantum Union Bound (Lemma 40), we have:

dtr​(|ψ′⟩,|ϕ⟩⊗|0n−t⟩)≤∑k=t+1n(1−λk)2.\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi^{\prime} },\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-t}})\leq\sqrt{\sum^{n}_{k=t+1}\frac{(1-\lambda_{k})}{2}}. (S82)

Therefore, by using the unitarity invariance of the trace-norm, we can conclude. ∎

From this, it readily follows that trace distance between the state and the set of tt-compressible pure Gaussian states 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} is upper bounded by:

min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≤(n−t)​(1−λt+1)2.\displaystyle\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\leq\sqrt{(n-t)\frac{(1-\lambda_{t+1})}{2}}. (S83)

V.2 Lower bound on the trace distance from the set of tt-compressible states

In this section, we establish a lower bound on the trace distance of a state from the set of tt-compressible Gaussian states. We denote the set of pure tt-compressible Gaussian states as 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}. In the following proof, we follow the derivation presented in Ref. [76] for the case of pure Gaussian states (t=0t=0), extending it to tt-compressible states.

Proposition 47.

Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be a quantum state, and let {λi}i=1n\{\lambda_{i}\}^{n}_{i=1} be the normal eigenvalues of its correlation matrix, ordered in increasing order. The lower bound on the trace distance between the state and the set of tt-compressible pure Gaussian states 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} is given by:

min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≥12​(1−λt+1)\displaystyle\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\geq\frac{1}{2}(1-\lambda_{t+1}) (S84)
Proof.

Consider an arbitrary operator OO with ‖O‖∞≤1\|O\|_{\infty}\leq 1, to be fixed later. Let |ϕt⟩∈𝒢t\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}. Then, we have:

dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t}) =12​‖|ψ⟩⟨ψ|−|ϕt⟩⟨ϕt|‖1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\|\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}-\outerproduct{\phi_t}{\phi_t}\|_{1} (S85)
≥12​|Tr⁡(O⁡(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|−|ϕt⟩⟨ϕt|))|,\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}|\Tr(O(\ketbra{\psi}- \ketbra{\phi_t}))|, (S86)

where in the last step, we used Holder’s inequality.

Let C⁡(|ψ⟩)C(\ket{\psi}) and C⁡(|ϕt⟩)C(\ket{\phi_t}) be the correlation matrices of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} and |ϕt⟩\ket{\phi_t}, respectively. Since C⁡(|ψ⟩)−C⁡(|ϕt⟩)C(\ket{\psi})-C(\ket{\phi_t}) is real and antisymmetric, it can be brought into its normal form C⁡(|ψ⟩)−C⁡(|ϕt⟩)=QT​Λ′​QC(\ket{\psi})-C(\ket{\phi_t})=Q^{T}\Lambda^{\prime}Q, where Λ′=⨁j=1ni​σj′​Y\Lambda^{\prime}=\bigoplus^{n}_{j=1}i\sigma^{\prime}_{j}Y and {σj′}j=1n\{\sigma^{\prime}_{j}\}^{n}_{j=1} are the normal eigenvalues of C⁡(|ψ⟩)−C⁡(|ϕt⟩)C(\ket{\psi})-C(\ket{\phi_t}) and Q∈O⁡(2​n)Q\in\mathrm{O}(2n) is an orthogonal matrix (Lemma 16).

Now, choose the operator OO in the form O=UQ†​i​γ2​k−1​γ2​k​UQO=U^{\dagger}_{Q}i\gamma_{2k-1}\gamma_{2k}U_{Q}, where k∈[n]k\in[n] and UQU_{Q} is a Gaussian unitary associated with the orthogonal matrix Q∈O⁡(2​n)Q\in\mathrm{O}(2n). Note that ‖O‖∞=1\|O\|_{\infty}=1. Fix kk as a value of jj that maximizes |σj′||\sigma_{j}^{\prime}|. Thus, we have:

|Tr⁡(O⁡(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|−|ϕt⟩⟨ϕt|))|\displaystyle|\Tr(O(\ketbra{\psi}- \ketbra{\phi_t}))| =|[C⁡(UQ​|ψ⟩)−C⁡(UQ​|ϕt⟩)]2​k−1,2​k|\displaystyle=|[C(U_{Q}\ket{\psi})-C(U_{Q}\ket{\phi_t})]_{2k-1,2k}| (S87)
=|[Q⁡(C⁡(|ψ⟩)−C⁡(|ϕt⟩))​QT]2​k−1,2​k|\displaystyle=|[Q(C(\ket{\psi})-C(\ket{\phi_t}))Q^{T}]_{2k-1,2k}| (S88)
=|σk′|\displaystyle=|\sigma_{k}^{\prime}| (S89)
=maxj∈[n]⁡|σj′|\displaystyle=\max_{j\in[n]}|\sigma_{j}^{\prime}| (S90)
=‖C⁡(|ψ⟩)−C⁡(|ϕt⟩)‖∞,\displaystyle=\|C(\ket{\psi})-C(\ket{\phi_t})\|_{\infty}, (S91)

where in the first step we used the definition of correlation matrix, in the second step we used Lemma 15 and in the last step we used the fact that the largest normal eigenvalues of an anti-symmetric matrix corresponds to the infinity norm of the matrix. Therefore, combining with (S86), we have:

dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≥12​‖C⁡(|ψ⟩)−C⁡(|ϕt⟩)‖∞.\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\geq\frac{1}{2}\|C(\ket{\psi})-C(\ket{\phi_t})\|_{\infty}. (S92)

Now, by applying Lemma 39, we have:

∥C(|ψ⟩)−C(|ϕt⟩)∥∞≥|λ(C(|ψ⟩)t+1−λ(C(|ϕt⟩)t+1|,\displaystyle\|C(\ket{\psi})-C(\ket{\phi_t})\|_{\infty}\geq|\lambda(C(\ket{\psi})_{t+1}-\lambda(C(\ket{\phi_t})_{t+1}|, (S93)

where λ​(C)t+1\lambda(C)_{t+1} denotes the t+1t+1-th smallest normal eigenvalue of a correlation matrix CC. Since |ϕt⟩\ket{\phi_t} is a tt-compressible Gaussian state, its Gaussian dimension is n−tn-t (because of Proposition 35), hence its t+1t+1-th smallest normal eigenvalue must be one. Therefore, the desired lower bound is obtained by taking the minimum over |ϕt⟩∈𝒢t\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t} . ∎

V.3 Testing the Gaussian dimension of a state

We present an efficient algorithm (Algorithm 2) for property testing of tt-compressible states, where 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} represents the set of nn-qubits tt-compressible Gaussian states, or equivalently the set of states with n−tn-t Gaussian dimension. The algorithm takes copies of a state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} as input and determines whether min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≤εA\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\leq\varepsilon_{A} or min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≥εB\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\geq\varepsilon_{B}, with the promise that one of these cases is true, where εB>εA≥0\varepsilon_{B}>\varepsilon_{A}\geq 0.

We provide the details of the testing algorithm in Algorithm 2. The correctness of this algorithm is established by the following theorem, the proof of which follows the same steps as proofs presented in [76].

Theorem 48 (Efficient tt-compressible Gaussian testing).

Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be an nn-qubit pure state. Assume εB,εA∈[0,1]\varepsilon_{B},\varepsilon_{A}\in[0,1] such that εB>(n−t)​εA\varepsilon_{B}>\sqrt{(n-t)\varepsilon_{A}}, δ∈(0,1]\delta\in(0,1], and εcorr=(εB2n−t−εA)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}=(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}_{B}}{n-t}-\varepsilon_{A}). Assume that |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is such that min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≤εA\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\leq\varepsilon_{A} or min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)>εB\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})>\varepsilon_{B}. Then, Algorithm 2 can discriminate between these two scenarios using N=⌈16​(n3/εcorr2)​log⁡(4​n2/δ)⌉N=\lceil 16(n^{3}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}^{2})\log(4n^2/\delta)\rceil single-copy measurements of the state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} with a probability of success at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Proof.

Let εcorr>0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}>0 be an accuracy parameter to be fixed later. By Lemma 38, with N≥8​(n3/εcorr2)​log⁡(4​n2/δ)N\geq 8(n^{3}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}^{2})\log(4n^2/\delta) single-copy measurements, we can find a matrix Γ^\hat{\Gamma} such that, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, it holds that ‖Γ^−Γ⁡(|ψ⟩)‖∞≤εcorr\norm{\hat{\Gamma}-\Gamma(\ket{\psi})}_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}. This implies that for all k∈[n]k\in[n], we have |λ^k−λk|≤εcorr|\hat{\lambda}_{k}-\lambda_{k}|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}, where {λ^k}k=1n,{λk}k=1n\{\hat{\lambda}_{k}\}^{n}_{k=1},\{\lambda_{k}\}^{n}_{k=1} are the normal eigenvalues of Γ^\hat{\Gamma} and Γ⁡(|ψ⟩)\Gamma(\ket{\psi}) respectively. Let εtest\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}} be a parameter to fix later. If λ^t+1≥1−εtest\hat{\lambda}_{t+1}\geq 1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}}, we aim to show that min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≤εB\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\leq\varepsilon_{B}, otherwise, we aim to show that min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)>εA\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})>\varepsilon_{A}. Thus, we first assume that λ^t+1≥1−εtest\hat{\lambda}_{t+1}\geq 1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}}. From Lemma 46, we have that:

min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≤(n−t)2​(1−λt+1)≤(n−t)2​(1−λ^t+1+εcorr)≤(n−t)2​(εtest+εcorr).\displaystyle\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\leq\sqrt{\frac{(n-t)}{2}(1-\lambda_{t+1})}\leq\sqrt{\frac{(n-t)}{2}(1-\hat{\lambda}_{t+1}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}})}\leq\sqrt{\frac{(n-t)}{2}(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}})}. (S94)

Therefore we need to ensure that (n−t)2​(εtest+εcorr)≤εB\sqrt{\frac{(n-t)}{2}(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}})}\leq\varepsilon_{B}. Let us analyze now the case in which λ^t+1<1−εtest\hat{\lambda}_{t+1}<1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}}. From Lemma 47, we have:

min|ϕt⟩∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(|ψ⟩,|ϕt⟩)≥12​(1−λt+1)≥12​(1−λ^t+1−εcorr)>12​(εtest−εcorr)\displaystyle\min_{\ket{\phi_t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\ket{\psi},\ket{\phi_t})\geq\frac{1}{2}(1-\lambda_{t+1})\geq\frac{1}{2}(1-\hat{\lambda}_{t+1}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}})>\frac{1}{2}(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}) (S95)

Therefore, we impose that εtest−εcorr2≥εA\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}}{2}\geq\varepsilon_{A}. The two mentioned inequalities are satisfied by choosing εtest=(εB2n−t+εA)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{test}}=(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}_{B}}{n-t}+\varepsilon_{A}) and εcorr=(εB2n−t−εA)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}=(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}_{B}}{n-t}-\varepsilon_{A}), by assuming that εB>(n−t)​εA\varepsilon_{B}>\sqrt{(n-t)\varepsilon_{A}}. ∎

Supplementary Material VI: Pseudorandomness from tt-doped Gaussian states and time complexity lower bound

We have presented an algorithm for learning tt-doped fermionic Gaussian states with a time complexity scaling as 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n,2t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(n,2^{t})) (assuming that the Majorana locality κ\kappa of each non-Gaussian gate is constant in the number of qubits). Thus, as long as t=𝒪⁡(log⁡(n))t=\mathcal{O}(\log(n)), the algorithm is efficient, i.e., the total run-time is polynomial in the number of qubits. In this section, we delve into establishing lower bounds on the time complexity for learning tt-doped fermionic Gaussian states. We begin by demonstrating that, under a well-believed cryptography assumption [73, 74, 46, 47, 75, 48], no algorithm can learn tt-doped fermionic Gaussian states with time complexity scaling in tt as 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(t)). This rules out efficient algorithms if tt scales polynomially with the number of qubits nn. However, under a stronger cryptography assumption [46, 47, 48, 49], we can establish that when tt scales slightly faster than logarithmically in the number of qubits nn, i.e., t=ω~​(log⁡(n))t=\tilde{\omega}(\log(n)), there exists no efficient algorithm to learn tt-doped fermionic Gaussian states, where we defined ω~​(log⁡(n))≔ω⁡(log⁡(n)​polyloglog​(n))\tilde{\omega}(\log(n))\coloneqq\omega\!\left(\log(n)\mathrm{polyloglog}(n)\right).

VI.1 tt-doped Gaussian states cannot be learned in polynomial time in tt

Our cryptography assumption relies on the conjecture that a specific problem, namely “Learning With Errors over Rings” 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} [73], is hard to solve by quantum computers [73, 74, 46, 47, 75, 48]. Detailed definitions and discussions about 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} can be found in [73]. Informally, 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} is a variant of the more general “Learning With Errors” (LWE) problem specialized to polynomial rings over finite fields, where the LWE problem is to distinguish random linear equations, perturbed by a small amount of noise, from truly uniform ones.

Crucial to our proof is a lemma, adapted from [72] (which strongly relies on previous work [46, 51, 50]), presented below:

Lemma 49 (Adapted from Theorem 14 in [72]).

Assume that 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} cannot be solved by quantum computers in polynomial time. Then, there exists a set 𝒮PRS\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{PRS}} of kk-qubits pure quantum states, known as pseudorandom quantum states, with the following properties:

  1. 1.

    Any state in 𝒮PRS\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{PRS}} can be prepared using 𝒪~​(k)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k) Toffoli and Hadamard gates (here, 𝒪~​(⋅)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot) hides polylog⁡(⋅)\mathrm{polylog(\cdot)} factors).

  2. 2.

    States in the set 𝒮PRS\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{PRS}} cannot be learned in time complexity 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(t)) by quantum computers. More specifically, let ρ∈𝒮PRS\rho\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{PRS}} be an unknown quantum state. Then there is no quantum algorithm that, using 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(k))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(k)) copies of ρ\rho and computational time, with probability at least 2/32/3 outputs a classical description of a state ρ^\hat{\rho} which can be prepared in polynomial time on a quantum computer such that dtr​(ρ,ρ^)≤1/8d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho,\hat{\rho})\leq 1/8.

Now we use this Lemma to show that there is no algorithm for learning tt-doped states with a 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(t)) computational time scaling in tt.

Proposition 50 (No poly⁡(t)\mathrm{poly}(t) algorithm to learn tt-doped states).

Assume that 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} cannot be solved by quantum computers in polynomial time. Then there is no quantum algorithm that, given access to copies of a tt-doped fermionic Gaussian nn-qubits state ρ\rho and with a time complexity scaling in tt as 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(t)), outputs a classical description of a quantum state ρ^\hat{\rho} such that it can be prepared in polynomial time on a quantum computer and, with probability at least 2/32/3, it holds that dtr​(ρ,ρ^)≤1/8d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho,\hat{\rho})\leq 1/8.

Proof.

Consider an nn-qubit state of the form |ϕ⟩⊗|0n−k⟩\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-k}}, where |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is a kk-qubit state in the set 𝒮PRS\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{PRS}} defined in Lemma 49. Let |ϕ⟩=UPRS​|0k⟩\ket{\phi}=U_{\mathrm{PRS}}\ket{0^k}, prepared by a unitary UPRSU_{\mathrm{PRS}} that can be implemented using 𝒪~​(k)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k) Hadamard and Toffoli gates, as per Lemma 49. The Toffoli gates can be implemented in turn using Hadamard, CNOT, T-gates, and T-gates inverse. For each gate in the system, utilizing a standard SWAP-exchange trick, we can make any gate acting on some qubits of the system to act only on the first two qubits through a cascade of SWAP gates. This incurs a total overhead factor of 𝒪⁡(k)\mathcal{O}(k) in the total number of gates. The SWAP gates between nearest-neighbor qubits are local non-Gaussian gates, since they can be expressed as SWAPi,i+1=e−i​π4​exp⁡(i​π4​(Xi​Xi+1+Yi​Yi+1+Zi​Zi+1))\text{SWAP}_{i,i+1}=e^{-i\frac{\pi}{4}}\exp(i\frac{\pi}{4}(X_iX_{i+1}+Y_iY_{i+1}+Z_iZ_{i+1})), which have Majorana locality equal to 44 (due to the Jordan-Wigner mapping). Also the other gates, now acting on the first two qubits, are (possibly) non-Gaussian gates with Majorana locality at most 44. This is because the Pauli operators in the generator of each gate can be expressed in terms of Majorana operators via the Jordan-Wigner transformation. This results in a total of t=𝒪~​(k2)t=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k^{2}) local non-Gaussian gates required to prepare the state. Thus, the |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} is a tt-doped Gaussian state with κ=4\kappa=4 Majorana local non-Gaussian gates. Now, due to Lemma 49, there exists no learning algorithm to learn such a state in time 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(k))=𝒪⁡(poly⁡(t))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(k))=\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(t)), with error less than 1/81/8 and probability of success at least 2/32/3. ∎

VI.2 Learning ω~​(log⁡(n))\tilde{\omega}(\log(n))-doped Gaussian states is hard

The previous Proposition rules out efficient algorithms when t=Ω⁡(poly⁡(n))t=\Omega(\mathrm{poly}(n)). However, our proposed algorithm is not anymore efficient when t=ω~​(log⁡(n))t=\tilde{\omega}(\log(n)), while it is efficient for t=𝒪⁡(log⁡(n))t=\mathcal{O}(\log(n)). If we were to make the stronger assumption, namely that 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} cannot be solved by quantum computers in sub-exponential time [46, 47, 48, 49], then we can rule out that efficient algorithm for t=ω~​(log⁡(n))t=\tilde{\omega}(\log(n)) exists (which means faster than ω⁡(log⁡(n))\omega(\log(n)) but hiding polyloglog\mathrm{polyloglog} factors). For showing this, we need first the following Lemma adapted by [72].

Lemma 51 (Adapted from Theorem 14 and 15 in [72]).

Assume that 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} cannot be solved by quantum computers in sub-exponential time. Then, there exists a set 𝒮PRS\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{PRS}} of kk-qubit pure quantum states, known as pseudorandom quantum states, with the following properties:

  1. 1.

    Any state in 𝒮PRS\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{PRS}} can be prepared using 𝒪~​(k)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k) Toffoli and Hadamard gates (here, 𝒪~​(⋅)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot) hides polylog⁡(⋅)\mathrm{polylog}(\cdot) factors).

  2. 2.

    Any algorithm to learn states from the set 𝒮PRS\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{PRS}} must have exp⁡(Ω⁡(k))\exp(\Omega(k)) time complexity. More specifically, let ρ∈𝒮PRS\rho\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{PRS}} be an unknown quantum state. Then any quantum algorithm that, by querying copies of ρ\rho, with probability at least 2/32/3 outputs a classical description of a state ρ^\hat{\rho} which can be prepared in sub-exponential time on a quantum computer such that dtr​(ρ,ρ^)≤1/8d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho,\hat{\rho})\leq 1/8, must have exp⁡(Ω⁡(k))\exp(\Omega(k)) time-complexity.

Now we use this to prove the following Proposition, also stated informally in the main text as Theorem 5. It reaches stronger conclusion than Proposition 50, but at the cost of stronger cryptography assumption. The idea of the following proof is to use a more compact qubits-to-fermion mapping than Jordan-Wigner, namely a modification of the one introduced by Kitaev [25], which would allow to create pseudorandom quantum states with no overhead in the number of non-Gaussian gates compared to the number of Toffoli and Hadamard gates. In the following, we recall that ω~​(log⁡(n))\tilde{\omega}(\log(n)) is defined as ω~​(log⁡(n)):=ω⁡(log⁡(n)​polyloglog​(n))\tilde{\omega}(\log(n)):=\omega(\log(n)\mathrm{polyloglog}(n))).

Proposition 52 (Learning ω~​(log⁡(n))\tilde{\omega}(\log(n))-doped Gaussian states is hard).

Assume that 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} cannot be solved by quantum computers in sub-exponential time. Then, there is no efficient (i.e., 𝒪⁡(poly⁡(n))\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}(n)) time) quantum algorithm that, by querying copies of a ω~​(log⁡(n))\tilde{\omega}(\log(n))-doped Gaussian state ρ\rho, with probability at least 2/32/3 outputs a description of a state ρ^\hat{\rho} which can be prepared in polynomial time on a quantum computer such that dtr​(ρ,ρ^)≤1/8d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho,\hat{\rho})\leq 1/8.

Proof.

Following a similar approach as in the proof of Proposition 50, we begin by defining a state |ϕ⟩⊗|0n−k⟩\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^{n-k}}, where |ϕ⟩=UPRS​|0k⟩\ket{\phi}=U_{\mathrm{PRS}}\ket{0^k} represents a kk-qubit state in the set 𝒮PRS\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{PRS}} as defined in Lemma 51. This state can be efficiently prepared using a unitary UPRSU_{\mathrm{PRS}} with 𝒪~​(k)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k) Hadamard and Toffoli gates, which, in turn, can be implemented using Hadamard gates, CNOTs, T-gates, and their inverses. In contrast to the previous proof in Proposition 50, an application of the same argument would not yield the desired conclusion due to the unfavorable quadratic overhead introduced by the SWAP-exchange trick in the number of non-Gaussian gates. That trick was necessary due to the use of Jordan-Wigner transformation. However, we can employ a more efficient qubits-to-fermions mapping, specifically a modified version of the one introduced by Kitaev [25]. Hereafter, we will refer to it as the “Kitaev encoding.” Our objective is to construct a fermionic state encoding |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} using a circuit of size 𝒪~​(k)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k) composed of Gaussian and κ=4\kappa=4 local non-Gaussian gates. We employ a mapping of kk qubits into 2​k2k fermionic modes using Majorana operators {γα,j|j∈[k],α∈{0,x,y,z}}\{\gamma_{\alpha,j}\,|\,j\in[k],\,\alpha\in\{0,\,x,\,y,\,z\}\}. These 4​k4k Majorana operators are defined in terms of 4​k4k Pauli strings via Jordan-Wigner, with an arbitrarily fixed operator ordering. We are now going to leverage the formalism and basics of stabilizer codes, for more in-depth information, refer to [88]. The Kitaev encoding involves defining a stabilizer code of 2​k2k physical qubits encoded in kk logical qubits, characterized by the following kk stabilizer generators {sj}j=1k\{s_{j}\}^{k}_{j=1} and logical Pauli operators {XjKE,ZjKE}j=1k\{X^{\rm KE}_{j},Z^{\rm KE}_{j}\}^{k}_{j=1}:

sj\displaystyle s_{j} :=γ0,j​γx,j​γy,j​γz,j,\displaystyle:=\gamma_{0,j}\gamma_{x,j}\gamma_{y,j}\gamma_{z,j}, (S96)
XjKE\displaystyle X^{\rm KE}_{j} :=i​γy,j​γz,j,\displaystyle:=i\gamma_{y,j}\gamma_{z,j}, (S97)
ZjKE\displaystyle Z^{\rm KE}_{j} :=i​γx,j​γy,j.\displaystyle:=i\gamma_{x,j}\gamma_{y,j}. (S98)

for each j∈[k]j\in[k]. Note that these operators explicitly satisfy the algebraic conditions on stabilizer generators and logical Pauli operators. The Kitaev encoding is associated to a Clifford transformation VKEV_{\rm KE} such that:

VKE​Xj​VKE†\displaystyle V_{\rm KE}X_{j}V_{\rm KE}^{\dagger} =XjKE,\displaystyle=X^{\rm KE}_{j}, (S99)
VKE​Zj​VKE†\displaystyle V_{\rm KE}Z_{j}V_{\rm KE}^{\dagger} =ZjKE,\displaystyle=Z^{\rm KE}_{j}, (S100)

for each j∈[k]j\in[k], and:

VKE​Zj​VKE†\displaystyle V_{\rm KE}Z_{j}V_{\rm KE}^{\dagger} =sj,\displaystyle=s_{j}, (S101)

for each j∈{k+1,…,2​k}j\in\{k+1,\dots,2k\}. The last equation ensures that VKE​|02​k⟩V_{\rm KE}\ket{0^{2k}} is an eigenstate with +1+1 eigenvalue for each of the stabilizer generators {sj}j=1k\{s_{j}\}^{k}_{j=1}, while Eq.(S100) implies that VKE​|02​k⟩V_{\rm KE}\ket{0^{2k}} is an eigenstate with +1+1 eigenvalue for each {ZjKE}j=1k\{Z^{\rm KE}_{j}\}^{k}_{j=1}. Thus, VKE​|02​k⟩V_{\rm KE}\ket{0^{2k}} is a valid “logical zero” stabilizer state. Exploiting the fact that VKE​|02​k⟩V_{\rm KE}\ket{0^{2k}} is an eigenstate with +1+1 eigenvalues of {ZjKE}j=1k\{Z^{\rm KE}_{j}\}^{k}_{j=1} and {sj​ZjKE}j=1k\{s_{j}Z^{\rm KE}_{j}\}^{k}_{j=1}, its density matrix can be written as:

VKE​|02​k⟩⟨02​k|​VKE†=∏j=1k(I+sj​ZjKE2)​∏j=k2​k(I+ZjKE2)\displaystyle V_{\rm KE}\outerproduct{0^{2k}}{0^{2k}}V^{{\dagger}}_{\rm KE}=\prod^{k}_{j=1}\left(\frac{I+s_{j}Z^{\rm KE}_{j}}{2}\right)\prod^{2k}_{j=k}\left(\frac{I+Z^{\rm KE}_{j}}{2}\right) =∏j=1k(I−i​γ0,j​γz,j2)​∏j=k2​k(I+i​γx,j​γy,j2).\displaystyle=\prod^{k}_{j=1}\left(\frac{I-i\gamma_{0,j}\gamma_{z,j}}{2}\right)\prod^{2k}_{j=k}\left(\frac{I+i\gamma_{x,j}\gamma_{y,j}}{2}\right). (S102)

From this, we observe that VKE​|02​k⟩V_{\rm KE}\ket{0^{2k}} is a fermionic Gaussian state because it can be written in the form of Eq.(S4), noting that signed permutation matrices are orthogonal matrices. Moreover, we denote YjKE:=−i​ZjKE​XjKE=i​γx,j​γz,jY^{\rm KE}_{j}:=-iZ^{\rm KE}_{j}X^{\rm KE}_{j}=i\gamma_{x,j}\gamma_{z,j}. The Kitaev encoding, as defined, ensures that the local qubit gates are mapped onto local fermionic ones. In particular, the gates of the circuit UPRSU_{\rm PRS} that prepares the pseudorandom state |ϕ⟩=UPRS​|0k⟩\ket{\phi}=U_{\rm PRS}\ket{0^k}— the Hadamard H\operatorname{H}, CNOT\operatorname{CNOT}, and T\operatorname{T}-gate — are, up to an overall phase, mapped onto

HjKE\displaystyle\mathrm{H}^{\rm KE}_{j} :=VKE​Hj​VKE†=VKE​(Zj​I+i​Yj2)​VKE†=ZjKE​I+i​YjKE2=e−π2​γx,j​γy,j​e−π4​γz,j​γx,j,\displaystyle:=V_{\rm KE}\mathrm{H}_{j}V_{\rm KE}^{\dagger}=V_{\rm KE}\left(Z_{j}\frac{I+iY_{j}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)V_{\rm KE}^{\dagger}=Z^{\rm KE}_{j}\frac{I+iY^{\rm KE}_{j}}{\sqrt{2}}=e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}\gamma_{x,j}\gamma_{y,j}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{4}\gamma_{z,j}\gamma_{x,j}}, (S103)

for each j≠l∈[k]j\neq l\in[k]. The only non-Gaussian among these is the encoding of the CNOT\mathrm{CNOT} gate, which has Majorana locality κ=4\kappa=4. This implies that the encoding of the circuit UPRSU_{\mathrm{PRS}}, i.e. UPRSKE:=VKE​UPRS​VKE†U^{\rm KE}_{\mathrm{PRS}}:=V_{\rm KE}U_{\mathrm{PRS}}V^{{\dagger}}_{\rm KE}, is a tt-doped fermionic Gaussian unitary with local non-Gaussian gates and t=𝒪~​(k)t=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k). Thus, we have that the Kitaev encoding of the pseudorandom state |ϕ⟩=UPRS​|0k⟩\ket{\phi}=U_{\mathrm{PRS}}\ket{0^k} is:

|ϕ⟩KE:=VKE​|ϕ⟩⊗|0k⟩=VKE​UPRS​|02​k⟩=UPRSKE​VKE​|02​k⟩.\displaystyle\ket{\phi}_{\rm KE}:=V_{\rm KE}\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^k}=V_{\rm KE}U_{\mathrm{PRS}}\ket{0^{2k}}=U^{\rm KE}_{\mathrm{PRS}}V_{\rm KE}\ket{0^{2k}}. (S106)

Since VKE​|02​k⟩V_{\rm KE}\ket{0^{2k}} is a Gaussian state and UPRSKEU^{\rm KE}_{\mathrm{PRS}} is a tt-doped Gaussian unitary with t=𝒪~​(k)t=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k), then VKE​|ϕ⟩⊗|0k⟩V_{\rm KE}\ket{\phi}\otimes\ket{0^k} is a tt-doped Gaussian state with t=𝒪~​(k)t=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k). The Majorana locality of each non-Gaussian gate is at most 44.

Using an arbitrary algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} for learning a tt-doped fermionic Gaussian state, we will now define a protocol for learning the pseudorandom state |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi}. Given a copy of a state |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} on kk qubits, we use kk auxiliary qubits in state |0⟩\ket{0} and apply the Clifford transformation VKEV_{\rm KE}. This means it can be produced by a circuit with O⁡(k2)O(k^{2}) 22-qubit gates [89]. The resulting |ϕ⟩KE\ket{\phi}_{\rm KE} can be input to 𝒜\mathcal{A} as a copy of a tt-doped fermionic Gaussian state for t=𝒪~​(k)t=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k). Using the number of copies of |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} given by sample complexity of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, we learn a description of a state ρ^KE\hat{\rho}_{\rm KE} which, with probability at least 2/32/3, satisfies:

dtr​(ρ^KE,ρKE)≤18,\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\hat{\rho}_{\rm KE},\rho_{\rm KE})\leq\frac{1}{8}, (S107)

where we defined ρKE\rho_{\rm KE} to be the density matrix associated with |ϕ⟩KE\ket{\phi}_{\rm KE}. By defining ρ^:=Tr{k+1,…,2​k}⁡(VKE†​ρ^KE​VKE)\hat{\rho}:=\Tr_{\{k+1,\dots,2k\}}\left(V^{{\dagger}}_{\rm KE}\hat{\rho}_{\rm KE}V_{\rm KE}\right), where Tr{k+1,…,2​k}⁡(⋅)\Tr_{\{k+1,\dots,2k\}}(\cdot) indicates the partial trace with respect to the qubits {k+1,…,2​k}\{k+1,\dots,2k\}, we also have:

dtr​(ρ^,|ϕ⟩⟨ϕ|)≤dtr​(VKE†​ρ^KE​VKE,|ϕ⟩⟨ϕ|⊗|0k⟩⟨0k|)=dtr​(VKE†​ρ^KE​VKE,VKE†​ρKE​VKE)=dtr​(ρ^KE,ρKE)≤18,\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\hat{\rho},\outerproduct{\phi}{\phi})\leq d_{\mathrm{tr}}(V^{{\dagger}}_{\rm KE}\hat{\rho}_{\rm KE}V_{\rm KE},\outerproduct{\phi}{\phi}\otimes\outerproduct{0^k}{0^k})=d_{\mathrm{tr}}(V^{{\dagger}}_{\rm KE}\hat{\rho}_{\rm KE}V_{\rm KE},V^{{\dagger}}_{\rm KE}\rho_{\rm KE}V_{\rm KE})=d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\hat{\rho}_{\rm KE},\rho_{\rm KE})\leq\frac{1}{8}, (S108)

where in the first step we used that the partial trace does not increase the trace distance between two states [90]. Hence, we found a state ρ^\hat{\rho} which is in trace distance close to the target state |ϕ⟩⟨ϕ|\outerproduct{\phi}{\phi}. To recap, we produced the learning algorithm for a pseudorandom state |ϕ⟩\ket{\phi} from a learning algorithm for tt-doped fermionic Gaussian states. The pseudorandom state learning algorithm has the same sample complexity as the fermionic one, and the time complexity TPRS=Sf⋅O⁡(k2)+TfT_{\rm PRS}=S_{\rm f}\cdot O(k^{2})+T_{\rm f} where TfT_{\rm f} and SfS_{\rm f} are time and sample complexity of the fermionic learner. If there is a fermionic learner whose time and sample complexity scale subexponentially in kk, the same property carries over to the pseudorandom states learner. By Lemma 51, this would contradict the cryptographic assumption that 𝖱𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖫𝖶𝖤\mathsf{RingLWE} cannot be solved by quantum computers in sub-exponential time. Hence, the time complexity of the fermionic learner needs to be exp⁡(Ω⁡(k))\exp(\Omega(k)). If k=ω⁡(log⁡(n))k=\omega(\log(n)), then this implies that any algorithm to learn tt-doped fermionic Gaussian states with t=𝒪~​(k)=ω⁡(log⁡(n)​polyloglog​(n))t=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(k)=\omega(\log(n)\mathrm{polyloglog}(n)) must be inefficient, i.e., its time complexity must be ω⁡(poly⁡(n))\omega(\mathrm{poly}(n)). ∎

Supplementary Material VII: Generalization to the mixed-state scenario and noise-robustness of the algorithm

Many of the concepts introduced in our work can be extended to the more realistic mixed-state scenario. We start by providing the definition for tt-compressible mixed states.

Definition 53 (Mixed tt-compressible state).

A possibly mixed state ρ\rho is a tt-compressible (Gaussian) state if and only if it can be represented as

ρ=G⁡(σ⊗|0n−t⟩⟨0n−t|)​G†,\displaystyle\rho=G(\sigma\otimes\outerproduct{0^{n-t}}{0^{n-t}})G^{{\dagger}}, (S109)

where GG is a Gaussian operation, and σ\sigma is a state supported solely on the first tt qubits.

As in the pure-state scenario (Proposition 35), saying that a quantum state is tt-compressible is equivalent to the fact that at least n−tn-t normal eigenvalues of the state’s correlation matrix are equal to one (i.e., its Gaussian dimension is ≥n−t\geq n-t and its Gaussian nullity is ≤t\leq t).

Proposition 54 (Equivalent definition of tt-compressible state).

A possibly mixed nn-qubit state ρ\rho is tt-compressible if and only if at least n−tn-t normal eigenvalues of the correlation matrix of ρ\rho are equal to one.

The proof is analogous to that of Proposition 35.

For the tomography algorithm, analogous guarantees extend from the tt-compressible pure-case to the tt-compressible mixed-state scenario. In this case, the unknown state is promised to be a tt-compressible Gaussian (possibly mixed) state. However, in this mixed-state scenario, the algorithm is simpler, since measuring the last n−tn-t qubits in the computational basis is not necessary because we do not require the output state to be pure, i.e., step 5 in Algorithm 1 is not necessary. Instead, the full state tomography of the first tt qubits can be applied right after having applied the Gaussian operation to the state. We explicitly show this in Algorithm 3 of the following subsection, whose proof of correctness is shown in the (more general) Theorem 57.

Furthermore, the following inequalities can be helpful to test how much a possibly mixed state ρ\rho deviates (in trace distance) from the set of mixed tt-compressible Gaussian states.

Proposition 55 (Minimum distance between a possibly mixed state and the set of tt-compressible states).

Let ρ\rho be a possibly mixed quantum state, and let {λi}i=1n\{\lambda_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} be the normal eigenvalues of its correlation matrix, ordered in increasing order. The following trace distance upper and lower bounds between the state and the set of tt-compressible mixed Gaussian states 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t} hold:

∑k=t+1n(1−λk)2≥minσt∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(ρ,σt)≥12​(1−λt+1).\displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{k=t+1}^{n}\frac{(1-\lambda_{k})}{2}}\geq\min_{\sigma_{t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho,\sigma_{t})\geq\frac{1}{2}(1-\lambda_{t+1}). (S110)

The proof of this theorem is analogous to those of Proposition 46 and Proposition 47, which held for the pure-state scenario but readily apply to the more general mixed-state scenario.

Thus, with the previous inequalities in hand, we can also provide a property testing algorithm that applies to a possibly mixed quantum state.

Theorem 56 (Efficient tt-compressible Gaussian testing).

Let ρ\rho be an nn-qubit possibly mixed quantum state. Assume εB,εA∈[0,1]\varepsilon_{B},\varepsilon_{A}\in[0,1] such that εB>(n−t)​εA\varepsilon_{B}>\sqrt{(n-t)\varepsilon_{A}}, δ∈(0,1]\delta\in(0,1], and εcorr=(εB2n−t−εA)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}=\left(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}_{B}}{n-t}-\varepsilon_{A}\right). Assume that ρ\rho is such that minσt∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(ρ,σt)≤εA\min_{\sigma_{t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho,\sigma_{t})\leq\varepsilon_{A} or minσt∈𝒢t⁡dtr​(ρ,σt)>εB\min_{\sigma_{t}\in\mathcal{G}_{t}}d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\rho,\sigma_{t})>\varepsilon_{B}. Then, Algorithm 2 can discriminate between these two scenarios using N=⌈16​(n3/εcorr2)​log⁡(4​n2/δ)⌉N=\lceil 16(n^{3}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr}}^{2})\log(4n^2/\delta)\rceil single-copy measurements of the state ρ\rho with a probability of success at least 1−δ1-\delta.

The proof of this theorem is similar to that of Theorem 48.

VII.1 Tomography of approximately tt-compressible states

In this subsection, we address the problem of tomography for ‘approximate tt-compressible states’, i.e., states with n−tn-t normal eigenvalues of their correlation matrix that are not exactly one, but almost.

This approach is particularly useful for the tomography of states where most of the normal eigenvalues are very close to one, such as states obtained when considering impurity models [45], as we will explore in more detail in the next section. Moreover, when preparing a target tt-compressible state in a quantum device (e.g., a target pure state prepared by a 1D matchgate circuit doped with a few SWAP gates), noise can cause an effective state ρ\rho to be prepared instead of the target tt-compressible state. Therefore, an algorithm that allows for perturbations from the set of tt-compressible states is experimentally motivated.

We provide such an algorithm in Table 3. Note that this differs from Algorithm 1 because in this mixed-state scenario we do not need to measure the last n−tn-t qubits in the computational basis before performing full-state tomography on the first tt qubits.

Theorem 57 (Efficient learning of approximate tt-compressible Gaussian states).

Let ε,δ∈(0,1]\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1]. Let ρ\rho be a quantum state. By utilizing N=𝒪⁡(n5ε4​log⁡(n2δ))+Ntom​(t,ε2,δ2)N=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{n^{5}}{\varepsilon^{4}}\log\!\left(\frac{n^{2}}{\delta}\right)\right)+N_{\mathrm{tom}}\!\left(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{2}\right) single-copy measurements and T=𝒪⁡(n3)+Ttom​(t,ε2,δ2)T=\mathcal{O}(n^{3})+T_{\mathrm{tom}}\!\left(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{2}\right) computational time, Algorithm 3 yields a classical representation of a state ρ^\hat{\rho}, satisfying

dtr​(ρ^,ρ)≤ε+εt,\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\hat{\rho},\rho)\leq\varepsilon+\varepsilon_{t}, (S111)

with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta. Here, εt≔∑j=t+1n(1−λj)/2\varepsilon_{t}\coloneqq\sqrt{\sum^{n}_{j=t+1}(1-\lambda_{j})/2}, where {λj}j=1n\{\lambda_{j}\}^{n}_{j=1} are the normal eigenvalues of the correlation matrix of ρ\rho ordered in increasing order. Moreover, Ntom​(t,ε2,δ2)N_{\mathrm{tom}}(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{2}) and Ttom​(t,ε2,δ2)T_{\mathrm{tom}}(t,\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\frac{\delta}{2}) respectively denote the number of copies and computational time sufficient for full-state tomography of a mixed tt-qubit state with an ε/2\varepsilon/2 accuracy and a failure probability of at most δ/2\delta/2.

Proof.

The learning procedure is outlined in Algorithm 3 and we now establish its correctness. According to Lemma 38, Nc​(n,εc,δ/2)N_{c}(n,\varepsilon_{c},\delta/2) single copies of ρ\rho are sufficient to construct an anti-symmetric real matrix C^\hat{C} such that ‖C^−C‖∞≤εc\norm{\hat{C}-C}_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon_{c} with a probability of at least 1−δ/21-\delta/2, where CC is the correlation matrix of ρ\rho. Then, we can put C^\hat{C} in its normal form C^=O^​Λ^​O^T\hat{C}=\hat{O}\hat{\Lambda}\hat{O}^{T}, where O^∈O⁡(2​n)\hat{O}\in\mathrm{O}(2n) is an orthogonal matrix and Λ^\hat{\Lambda} is a matrix of the form Λ^=i​⨁j=1nλj​(C^)​Y\hat{\Lambda}=i\bigoplus^{n}_{j=1}\lambda_{j}(\hat{C})Y, where {λj​(C^)}j=1n\{\lambda_{j}(\hat{C})\}^{n}_{j=1} are the normal eigenvalues of C^\hat{C}. For m∈{t+1,…,n}m\in\{t+1,\dots,n\}, we have:

where Zm=−i​γ2​m−1​γ2​mZ_{m}=-i\gamma_{2m-1}\gamma_{2m} is the ZZ-Pauli operator acting on the mm-th qubit. In the second step we used that that |C​(ψ′)j,k−(Λ^)j,k|≤εc\lvert C(\psi^{\prime})_{j,k}-(\hat{\Lambda})_{j,k}\rvert\leq\varepsilon_{c}, as follows by C⁡(ρ′)=O^T​C​(ρ)​O^C(\rho^{\prime})=\hat{O}^{T}C(\rho)\hat{O}, Λ^=O^T​C^​O^\hat{\Lambda}=\hat{O}^{T}\hat{C}\hat{O}, Cauchy-Schwarz and the definition of infinity norm. Tr⁡(|0⟩⟨0|m​ρ′)=12+12​Tr⁡(Zm​ρ′)≥1−(εc+1−λm​(C)2).\displaystyle\Tr(\ketbra{0}{0}_m \rho^{\prime})=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\Tr(Z_m \rho^{\prime})\geq 1-(\varepsilon_{c}+\frac{1-\lambda_{m}(C)}{2}). (S116)

dtr​(ρ^,ρ)≤ε2+2​ε216+εt2≤ε+εt,\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{tr}}(\hat{\rho},\rho)\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+2\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{16}+\varepsilon^{2}_{t}}\leq\varepsilon+\varepsilon_{t}, (S128)
